q2.a: Training is the act of increasing the new skills of problem solving and technical knowledge of an employee for doing the jobs. According to Edwin B. Flippo, "Training is the act of increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing particular jobs."

Mentoring is the process of sharing knowledge and experience by a senior person with an employee. It focuses on the development of attitude of trainees and is mostly used for managerial employees. It is one-to-one interaction; the mentor provides support and feedback.

Under role play, trainees are explained the situation and assigned roles. They have to act out the roles without any rehearsal or pre-prepared dialogues, e.g. customer and salesman, management and union leader. The moderator gives his views after observing.

E-learning is the use of technology to access training outside a traditional classroom or office. It is also called online learning or web-based training. Information can pass over the internet anywhere and any time, saving lakhs of rupees for organisations.

q3.q: What is vestibule training?
q3.a:
- Vestibule training is training of employees in an environment similar to the actual work environment, artificially created for training purpose.
- It avoids damage or loss to machinery by trainees and avoids disturbing normal workflow.
- It is given to drivers, pilots, space scientists etc.

q3.q: What do you mean by on the job Training?
q3.a:
- On-the-job training is given to the employee at the work place by his immediate supervisor; the employee learns the job in the actual work environment.
- It is based on the principle of "Learning by Doing and Learning While Earning".
- It is suitable for skills that can be learnt in a short period.
- Methods: coaching, mentoring, job rotation, JIT, apprenticeship, committee assignment, understudy.

q3.q: Write down various steps in a training programme.
q3.a:
1. Whom to train? – operational, supervisory or executive level.
2. Who is the trainee? – selected on self-interest and recommendation.
3. Who are trainers? – supervisors, co-workers, HR staff, consultants, faculty.
4. What method will be used for training?
5. What should be the level of training? – introductory, skill development or higher level.
6. Where to conduct the training programme? – venue and duration.

q3.q: Write short note on trainer and trainee.
q3.a:
- **Trainee:** A person who is learning and practising the skills of a particular job. Trainees are selected on the basis of self-interest and recommendation by the supervisor or HR department.
- **Trainer:** A person who teaches skills to employees and prepares them for a job. Trainers may be supervisors, co-workers, HR staff, specialists, outside consultants, industry associations or faculty of universities. A trainer is also called instructor, coach, teacher, mentor, adviser, counsellor, guide, guru or tutor.

q5.q: Discuss various types of training. (any 5)
q5.a:
**On-the-job methods**
1. **Coaching:** superior guides the new employee, points out mistakes and suggests remedies.
2. **Mentoring:** senior shares knowledge and experience one-to-one; develops attitude.
3. **Job rotation:** trainee is shifted periodically from one job/department to another to learn inter-related jobs.
4. **Job Instruction Technique:** supervisor instructs how to do the job and its purpose.
5. **Apprenticeship:** trainee learns from a senior worker for 1–5 years with stipend – mechanics, electricians, welders.
6. **Committee assignment:** employees learn by participating in decision making in committees.
7. **Understudy/Internship:** subordinate learns by assisting a superior in day-to-day problems.
**Off-the-job methods**
1. **Lecture:** concepts and theories explained with audio-visual tools.
2. **Group discussion:** groups discuss an issue and present solutions.
3. **Case study:** trainees apply knowledge to solve a described situation.
4. **Role play:** acting out assigned roles without rehearsal.
5. **Seminar/Conference:** lectures, interaction and paper presentation.
6. **Field trip:** visit to actual work sites for exposure.
7. **Vestibule training:** artificial work environment – pilots, drivers.
8. **E-learning:** web-based training.
9. **Demonstration:** trainer shows how to do the task.
10. **Programmed instruction:** units from simple to complex with self-evaluation and feedback.

q5.q: What are the difference between on the job training and off the job training? (any 5)
q5.a:
| Basis | On the Job Training | Off the Job Training |
| Meaning | Employee learns in the actual work environment | Training outside the actual work location |
| Cost | Cheapest | Expensive – separate rooms, specialists, projectors |
| Location | At the work place | Away from the work place |
| Suitable for | Manufacturing/production jobs | Managerial and non-production jobs |
| Approach | Practical | Theoretical |
| Principle | Learning by performing | Learning by acquiring knowledge |
| Carried out by | Experienced employee | Experts |
| Deals with | Day-to-day job requirements | Groups of workers at the same time |
| Work disturbance | More distraction (noise, machines) | No distraction |
| Methods | Coaching, job rotation, apprenticeship, mentoring | Role play, seminar, lecture, case study, vestibule |

q5.q: Explain the benefits of training. (2 points from each headings)
q5.a:
**(i) To the organisation**
- Improves skill of employees and enhances productivity and profitability.
- Reduces wastage of materials and idle time.
- Exposes employees to latest trends; minimises supervision.
- Reduces accidents, labour turnover; improves union–management relations.
**(ii) To the employees**
- Adds to knowledge, skill and competency.
- Quick promotion and career advancement.
- Improves productivity, morale and earnings through incentives.
- Builds confidence and positive attitude; safety practices.
**(iii) To customers**
- Better quality of product/service.
- Innovative, value-added or feature-rich products.

q5.q: Explain the need for training.
q5.a:
1. **Improved quality of work.**
2. **Enhance employee growth** through new skills.
3. **Prevention of obsolescence** – learn latest technology (the major purpose).
4. **Enlightening new recruits** about methods, tools and culture.
5. **Improved safety measures.**
6. **Motivating employees** and building commitment.
7. **Higher productivity and profits.**
8. **Cost reduction** – no wastage.
9. **Reduced supervision.**
10. **Better adaptability** to new technology.

tips: Vestibule = artificial environment (pilots). Apprenticeship = technical cadre with stipend.

com.title: Concept of Market and Marketer
com.intro: A market is the meeting place of buyers and sellers. This chapter explains the meaning and need of markets, their classification, the marketer, what can be marketed, and the roles and functions of a marketer.

pts: From Latin **'Marcatus'** – trade, commerce, merchandise.
**Pyle:** "Market includes both place and region in which buyers and sellers are in free competition with one another."
**Clark and Clark:** "A market is a centre or an area in which the forces leading to exchange title to a particular product operate and towards which the actual goods tend to travel."
Exchange goods, adjust demand & supply by price, improve quality of life, new modes of life, develop products.
**Area:** Family, Local, National, International.
**Commodities:** Commodity market (produce exchange, manufactured goods, bullion) and Capital market (money, foreign exchange, stock).
**Economics:** Perfect, Imperfect.
**Transaction:** Spot, Future.
**Regulation:** Regulated, Unregulated.
**Time:** Very short period, Short period, Long period.
**Volume:** Wholesale, Retail.
**Importance:** Primary, Secondary, Terminal.
Goods, Services, Experiences, Events, Persons, Places, Properties, Organisations, Information, Ideas.
Instigator, Innovator, Integrator, Implementer.

Gathering market information, Market planning, Product design, Standardisation & grading, Packaging & labelling, Branding, Customer support, Pricing, Promotion & selling, Physical distribution, Transportation, Storage & warehousing.
TN examples: Goat market – Aathur; Flower market – Hosur.

terms: Meeting place of buyers and sellers in an area.
One who promotes or exchanges goods or services for money.
Market organised, controlled and regulated by statutory measures.
Goods exchanged and physical delivery takes place immediately.
Market for purchase and sale of gold and silver.
Central site for assembling and trading commodities in a metropolitan area.

q2.a: The word market is derived from the Latin word 'Marcatus' which means trade, commerce, merchandise, a place where business is transacted. In simple words, the meeting place of buyers and sellers in an area is called market. According to Pyle, "Market includes both place and region in which buyers and sellers are in free competition with one another."

"A person whose duties include the identification of the goods and services desired by a set of consumers, as well as the marketing of those goods and services on behalf of a company." – Business Dictionary.

q2.q: What is mean by Regulated Market?
q2.a: Regulated markets are markets which are organised, controlled and regulated by statutory measures. Example: Stock Exchanges of Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata.

q2.q: What is meant by Spot Market?
q2.a: In spot markets, goods are exchanged and the physical delivery of goods takes place immediately.

q2.q: What is meant by Commodity Market?
q2.a: A commodity market is a place where produced goods or consumption goods are bought and sold. It is sub-divided into produce exchange market, manufactured goods market and bullion market.

q3.q: What can be marketed in the Market? (any 3)
q3.a:
- **Goods:** consumer durables, electronic products, machinery, computers.
- **Services:** banking, insurance, hospitality, tourism, consultation.
- **Experiences:** amusement park, theme park, mountaineering.
- **Events:** exhibitions, fairs, World Cup, Olympics, T20.
- **Persons:** celebrities endorsing brands.
- **Places, Properties, Organisations, Information, Ideas.**

q3.q: Mention any three Role of Marketer?
q3.a:
- **Instigator:** watches market developments, identifies opportunities and leads the business in new directions.
- **Innovator:** distinguishes products by adding features, modifying pricing, new delivery patterns and business models.
- **Integrator:** collects feedback from channel members and consumers and provides solutions by co-ordinating functions.
- **Implementer:** converts marketing opportunities into marketable products with functional teams.

q3.q: Explain the types of market on the basis of time.
q3.a:
- **Very short period market:** deals in perishable goods like fruits, milk, vegetables; supply cannot change; price is determined by demand.
- **Short period market:** supply is adjusted to meet demand to some extent; demand is greater than supply.
- **Long period market:** deals in durable goods and services used for a longer period.

q5.q: How the market can be classified? (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Geographical area:** Family market (within family), Local market (village/town – perishables), National market, International/World market.
2. **Commodities:** (a) Commodity market – produce exchange (Hapur wheat, Bombay cotton), manufactured goods (Kanpur leather), bullion (gold, silver) (b) Capital market – money market, foreign exchange market, stock market.
3. **Economics:** Perfect market and Imperfect market.
4. **Transaction:** Spot market (immediate delivery) and Future market (future delivery).
5. **Regulation:** Regulated market (statutory control) and Unregulated market (free market).
6. **Time:** Very short period, Short period and Long period market.
7. **Volume of business:** Wholesale market (bulk) and Retail market (small quantities).
8. **Importance:** Primary market (farm produce in villages), Secondary market (semi-finished goods, between wholesalers), Terminal market (central assembling site in metro areas).

q5.q: How the market can be classified on the basis of Economics?
q5.a:
**a. Perfect market** – conditions:
- Large number of buyers and sellers.
- Uniform prices throughout the market.
- Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of the market.
- Goods can move from one place to another without restriction.
- Goods are identical or homogeneous.
- Such markets are rarely found.
**b. Imperfect market** – when:
- Products are similar but not identical.
- Prices are not uniform.
- There is lack of communication.
- There are restrictions on movement of goods.

q5.q: Explain the functions of a marketer.
q5.a:
- Gathering and analysing market information
- Market planning
- Product designing and development
- Standardisation and grading
- Packaging and labelling
- Branding
- Customer support services
- Pricing of products
- Promotion and selling
- Physical distribution, transportation, storage and warehousing

tips: Roles of marketer = 4 I's: Instigator, Innovator, Integrator, Implementer.

com.title: Marketing and Marketing Mix
com.intro: Marketing covers all activities that move goods and services from producer to consumer to satisfy human wants. This chapter explains the evolution, concepts, objectives, importance and functions of marketing, and the 4 Ps of the marketing mix.

pts: Barter system → Production orientation → Sales orientation → Marketing orientation → Consumer orientation → Management orientation.
Make what you can sell, do not try to sell what you can make.
First create a customer, then create products.
Love your customers, not the products.
**Customer is supreme or king.**
Customer's preferences shape your decisions.
**American Marketing Association:** "Marketing is concerned with the people and the activities involved in the flow of goods and services from the producer to the consumer."
**Baker and Anshen:** "The end of all the marketing activities is the satisfaction of human wants."
**Exchange:** buying & assembling, selling.
**Physical supply:** transportation (place utility), storage & warehousing (time utility).
**Facilitating:** financing, risk bearing, market information, standardisation, grading, branding, packing, pricing.
G.B. Giles gave 7 functions: marketing research, planning, product development, advertisement & sales promotion, selling & distribution, after-sale service, public relations.
"Marketing mix is a pack of four sets of variables namely product variable, price variable, promotion variable, and place variable."
**4 Ps:** Product, Price, Place, Promotion. Modern mix adds People, Process, Programme, Performance.

terms: Activities involved in the flow of goods and services from producer to consumer.
Combination of Product, Price, Place and Promotion offered to target consumers.
Classification of standardised products into well-defined classes.
Establishing standards based on intrinsic qualities like size, colour, taste.
Giving a name or symbol to differentiate a product from competitors.
Wrapping and crating goods to protect them from breakage, leakage and spoilage.

q2.a: Marketing is the performance of business activities that direct the flow of goods and services from producer to ultimate user. According to the American Marketing Association, "Marketing is concerned with the people and the activities involved in the flow of goods and services from the producer to the consumer."

"Marketing mix is a pack of four sets of variables namely product variable, price variable, promotion variable, and place variable." – Jerome McCarthy. It is a marketing programme offered by a firm to its target consumers to earn profits through satisfaction of their wants.
Grading means classification of standardised products into certain well-defined classes.

q3.q: What are the objectives of marketing?
q3.a:
- Intelligent and capable application of modern marketing policies.
- To develop the marketing field.
- To develop guiding policies and their implementation for good results.
- To suggest solutions by studying marketing problems.
- To find sources of further information on market problems.
- To revive existing marketing functions if shortcomings are found.

q3.q: What are the concept of marketing?
q3.a:
- Make what you can sell, but do not try to sell what you can make.
- First create a customer, then create products.
- Love your customers and not the products.
- Customer is supreme or king.
- Customer's preferences shape your decisions.

q3.q: What do you mean by marketing mix? Write any two elements.
q3.a:
Marketing mix means a marketing programme offered by a firm to its target consumers to earn profits through satisfaction of their wants. It is a mixture of four ingredients – Product, Price, Place and Promotion.
- **Product:** the main element of marketing; without a product there can be no marketing.
- **Price:** the value of a product expressed in monetary terms; the amount charged for the product.

q3.q: Explain the importance of marketing to society.
q3.a:
- Connecting link between consumer and producer.
- Increases living standard and nation's income.
- Increases employment opportunities.
- Removes imbalance of supply by moving surplus to deficit areas.
- Creates form, place, time and possession utilities.

q5.q: Discuss about the Evolution of marketing. (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Barter system:** goods exchanged for goods without money.
2. **Production orientation:** producers concentrated on mass production for profit; cared little about customers.
3. **Sales orientation:** selling became dominant without efforts to satisfy consumer needs.
4. **Marketing orientation:** customers' importance realised but only as a means of disposing goods; aggressive advertising, personal selling and sales promotion used.
5. **Consumer orientation:** only products capable of satisfying tastes, preferences and expectations of consumers are brought to market – consumer satisfaction.
6. **Management orientation:** marketing assumes a managerial role to co-ordinate all business activities for planning, promoting and distributing want-satisfying products.

q5.q: Narrate the Elements of Marketing mix.
q5.a:
1. **Product:** The main element of marketing. Without a product there can be no marketing. Includes features, brand, service, innovation, packaging, style and image.
2. **Price:** The value of a product expressed in monetary terms – the amount charged. Includes list price, discount, terms and conditions.
3. **Place (Physical distribution):** Moves products from the place of production to the place of consumption at the right time – channel, inventory, distribution, logistics. Even an excellent product is wasted if not moved properly.
4. **Promotion:** Conveys special features and benefits to potential consumers – advertisement, sales promotion, sales force. Media: TV, radio, newspaper, magazine, internet, billboard.
The 4P matrix: marketing decisions fall into these four controllable categories; positioning the product carefully in each generates a better response.

q5.q: Explain the functions of marketing.
q5.a:
**1. Functions of exchange:** (a) buying and assembling (b) selling.
**2. Functions of physical supply:** (a) transportation – creates place utility by land, water, air (b) storage and warehousing – holding goods from production to consumption; warehouses create time utility.
**3. Facilitating functions:**
- Financing – long, medium and short term.
- Risk bearing – time, place, competition, change in demand, natural calamities, human and political risks.
- Market information – "all the facts, estimates, opinions used in marketing" (Clark and Clark).
- Standardisation, Grading, Branding, Packing and Pricing.

tips: Remember the 6 stages of evolution in order: Barter → Production → Sales → Marketing → Consumer → Management.

com.title: Recent Trends in Marketing
com.intro: Marketing has moved online and into new forms. This chapter explains e-commerce, e-business, e-marketing, e-tailing, and modern marketing types like green, social, rural, service, niche, viral, ambush, guerrilla, multilevel, referral and content marketing.

pts: **E-Commerce:** all activities facilitating exchange of goods done through the internet.
**E-Business:** all business transactions through internet – wider: supply chain management, order processing, CRM.
Marketing of products and services over internet and telecom networks (online, web, internet, digital marketing).
**Judy Strauss** gave the definition.
Objectives: expansion of market share, reduction of distribution & promotion expenses, higher brand awareness, strengthening database.
**E-tailing:** online retailing (B2C) through shopping websites.
**Green marketing:** environment-friendly products (eco / sustainable marketing). E.g. Toyota Prius.
**Social marketing:** marketing for social good – anti-tobacco, road safety, anti-plastic.
**Rural marketing:** two-way flow – FMCG to villages, farm produce to cities.
**Service marketing:** intangible services – banking, insurance, healthcare, tourism.
**Commodity exchange:** regulated market for contracts tied to commodity prices.
**Niche marketing:** one well-defined segment – "big fish in a small pond" (recliner cinemas, sports channels).
**Viral marketing:** messages spread like a virus person to person (YouTube, Hotmail).
**Ambush marketing:** linking a brand to an event without paying sponsorship.
**Guerrilla marketing:** unconventional low-budget street promotions using time, energy and imagination.
**Multilevel marketing:** distributors recruit new distributors ("downline") – Amway, Tupperware; also network marketing / pyramid selling.
**Referral marketing:** promotion through existing customers' referrals; word of mouth.
**Content marketing:** communicating without selling – "non-interruption marketing".

terms: Exchange of goods and services through internet and online environments.
Marketing of products and services over internet and telecom networks.
Selling goods through a shopping website to the ultimate consumer (B2C).
Directing all marketing efforts to one well-defined segment.
Connecting a product to an event without paying sponsorship.
Users pass on a marketing message to others, creating exponential growth.

q2.a: A service is any activity or benefit that one party offers to another which is essentially intangible and does not result in ownership. Service marketing is a specialised branch of marketing denoting the selling of services like telecommunication, banking, insurance, car rentals, healthcare, tourism, professional services and repairs.

Green marketing implies marketing environmentally friendly products. It involves developing and promoting products and services which satisfy customers' wants for quality, performance, affordable pricing and convenience without causing a detrimental impact on the environment. It is also called environmental, ecological, eco-friendly or sustainable marketing.

Ambush marketing is a technique whereby an advertiser seeks to connect his product to an event in the mind of potential customers without paying sponsoring expenses to the event. It is a method of building brands in covert ways.

Social marketing is the systematic application of marketing philosophy and techniques to achieve specific behavioural goals which ensure social good – anti-tobacco, anti-drug, anti-pollution, anti-dowry, road safety, protection of girl child, against plastic bags.

q3.q: What are the advantages of E-Marketing?
q3.a:
- **Any time market:** 24/7 service; consumers can shop anytime from anywhere.
- **Cheaper products:** direct contact between manufacturer and end consumer cuts intermediation cost.
- **Wide choice:** customers can buy whatever they want just by browsing various sites.

q3.q: Discuss the objectives E-Marketing. (Any 3)
q3.a:
- Expansion of market share.
- Reduction of distribution and promotional expenses.
- Achieving higher brand awareness.
- Strengthening database.

q3.q: Explain in detail about Niche marketing.
q3.a:
- Niche marketing is a strategy of directing all marketing efforts towards one well-defined segment of the population.
- The company finds needs of customers not served or under-served by competitors and develops solutions for them.
- A niche market does not mean a small market; it has a specific target audience with a specialised offering – "a big fish in a small pond".
- Examples: cinema halls with recliner seats; sports channels like STAR Sports and ESPN targeting sports enthusiasts.

q3.q: What are the disadvantages of E-Marketing?
q3.a:
- High cost of website design, software, hardware and online advertising.
- Not suitable for small businesses and customers in long distances.
- Companies hardly update information on websites.
- Security fears – buyers are afraid of misuse of credit cards.

q5.q: Explain in detail how traditional marketing differ from E-marketing.
q5.a:
| E-Marketing | Traditional Marketing |
| Very economical and faster way to promote products | Very expensive and takes more time |
| Easier to promote products globally in a short time | Expensive and time consuming to promote globally |
| Business can expand with minimum manpower | Needs more manpower |
| Products can be sold/bought 24×7 round the year | Not possible |
Also add:
- **E-marketing advantages:** any time market, cheaper products, wide choice.
- **E-marketing disadvantages:** high cost, unsuitable for small business, security fears.

q5.q: Disscuss any two new methods of marketing.
q5.a:
1. **Green marketing:** Marketing environmentally friendly products that satisfy customers' needs for quality, performance, price and convenience without harming the environment. It responds to global warming and non-biodegradable waste. Also called ecological or sustainable marketing. Example: Toyota's Prius hybrid.
2. **Multilevel marketing:** Direct sales companies encourage existing distributors to recruit new distributors. A distributor earns commission on his own sales and a percentage of sales of the distributors he recruits ("downline"). Also called network marketing, referral marketing or pyramid selling. Examples: Amway, Tupperware.
(Other methods you can write: Niche, Viral, Ambush, Guerrilla, Social, Rural, Service, Referral, Content marketing.)

tips: For "new methods of marketing", choose the two you can write most clearly with an example.

com.title: Consumerism
com.intro: The consumer is the most exploited constituent in business. This chapter explains who a consumer is, how consumers are exploited, consumerism, its importance and growth, consumer protection, related laws, the Consumer Protection Act 1986, and caveat emptor / caveat venditor.

pts: One who consumes goods manufactured and sold by others or created by nature, and one who avails services (banking, transport, insurance).

**Under CPA 1986:** a person who buys goods or services for a consideration paid/promised/partly paid or under deferred payment. A person buying for resale or commercial purpose is NOT a consumer (except for earning livelihood by self-employment).
Selling at higher price, Adulteration, Duplicate/spurious goods, Artificial scarcity, Sub-standard goods, Product risk, Warranty and services, Unsuitability of products, False advertisements.
Social force protecting and aiding the consumer; organised effort against unfair marketing practices.
Term coined in the early **1960s** in America. **L. Massie:** "Consumerism is an attempt to enhance the rights and powers of buyers in relation to sellers."
**Ralph Nader** – Father of the Consumer Movement.

Awakening and uniting consumers, discouraging unfair trade practices, protecting against exploitation, awakening government, implementing laws, providing information, discouraging anti-social activities.
Roles of Business, Government and Consumers.
UN guidelines for consumer protection – **9 April 1985**.
In force from **15.04.1987**; amended 1993. Three-tier machinery: District Forum, State Commission, National Commission.
National Consumer Day: 24 December; World Consumer Rights Day: **15 March**.
**Caveat Emptor** – "Let the buyer beware" (old rule).
**Caveat Venditor** – "Let the seller beware" (present rule; implied warranty of merchantability).

terms: One who buys goods or services for consideration, not for resale.
Social force designed to protect consumers' interests by organising them to pressure business.
Mixing or substituting undesirable material in food.
Showing "No stock" while holding stock to sell at higher price.

q2.a: A consumer is one who consumes goods manufactured and sold by others or created by nature and sold by others, and one who avails services such as banking, transport and insurance. Under the CPA 1986, a person who buys goods or services for a consideration paid, promised or partly paid is a consumer; a person who buys for resale or commercial purpose is not a consumer.

- Chemicals, detergent, chalk, urea, caustic soda are added to milk to make it dense and white.
- Chilli powder is adulterated with brick powder.
(Others: stones mixed with grains; papaya seeds added to black pepper; coffee powder with tamarind seed.)

'Caveat emptor' is a Latin term that means "let the buyer beware". The buyer assumes the risk that a product fails to meet expectations or has defects; the buyer has no recourse with the seller. Buyers are expected to inspect the product before buying.

Caveat venditor means "let the seller beware". Today most sales fall under this principle, by which goods are covered by an implied warranty of merchantability. Nearly all consumer products are guaranteed to work if used for their intended purpose.

q2.q: Write a short notes on Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
q2.a: The Central Government enacted the Consumer Protection Act in 1986; it came into force from 15.04.1987 and was amended in 1993 (COPRA). It protects consumers against defective goods, deficient services and unfair trade practices. It provides a three-tier machinery – District Forums, State Commissions and the National Commission – for redressal of disputes.

q3.q: What are the important legislations related to consumerism in India? (any 3)
q3.a:
- **Indian Contract Act, 1872** – binds people on promises made in contracts.
- **Sale of Goods Act, 1930** – protects against sellers not complying with warranties.
- **Essential Commodities Act, 1955** – protects against artificial shortages and black marketing.
- **Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954** – checks adulteration of food.
- **Weights and Measures Act, 1976** (now Legal Metrology Act, 2009) – against underweight.
- **Trademark Act 1999, Competition Act 2002, BIS (ISI) Act 1952, Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, Food Safety Standards Act 2006.**

q3.q: What is meant by artificial scarcity?
q3.a:
- Shopkeepers put up the board 'No Stock' in front of their shops even though there is plenty of stock.
- Consumers who are desperate have to pay a hefty price, giving unconscientious profit to sellers.
- Example: 'House Full' board in cinema houses while tickets are sold at higher price in black market.

q3.q: Write the importance of consumerism. (any 3)
q3.a:
- Awakening and uniting consumers.
- Discouraging unfair trade practices.
- Protecting against exploitation.
- Awakening the government.
- Effective implementation of consumer protection laws.
- Providing complete and latest information.
- Discouraging anti-social activities.

q5.q: How consumers are exploited? (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Selling at higher price:** price not commensurate with quality; artificial scarcity to push up prices.
2. **Adulteration:** mixing undesirable material in food – causes monetary loss and spoils health (e.g. brick powder in chilli powder).
3. **Duplicate or spurious goods:** duplicates of spare parts, medicines, watches, even currency notes.
4. **Artificial scarcity:** 'No Stock' board while holding stock; 'House Full' with black market tickets.
5. **Sub-standard goods:** poor quality contents in sealed packs; sellers avoid bills.
6. **Product risk:** no warning about dangers and precautions.
7. **Warranty and services:** free service denied on flimsy grounds; exorbitant repair charges.
8. **Unsuitability of products:** "unbreakable" items break; "leak proof" batteries leak.
9. **False advertisements:** false representation of quality, price, composition, performance.

q5.q: Explain the role of business in consumer protection. (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Avoidance of price hike** during shortage.
2. **Avoidance of hoarding** and black marketing.
3. **Guarantees for good quality** – no false warranty.
4. **Product information** – correct details of size, quality, quantity, side effects, precautions.
5. **Truth in advertising** – no false or bogus information.
6. **Protection from hazard** – test safety; withdraw contaminated food.
7. **Money refund guarantee** – replace defective product or refund price.
8. **Consumer grievances** – handle complaints within a definite time frame.

q5.q: What are the objectives of Consumer Protection Act, 1986? (any 5)
q5.a:
1. Protection against marketing of goods hazardous to life and property.
2. Providing correct and complete information about quality, quantity, purity, price and standard of goods.
3. Protecting consumers from unfair trade practices.
4. Empowering consumers to seek redressal against exploitation.
5. Educating consumers of their rights and duties.
6. Ensuring a better standard of living with quality products at fair price.
7. Putting in place mechanisms like councils and authorities to enforce consumer rights.

q5.q: Explain the salient features of the Consumer Protection Act 1986.
q5.a:
- Protecting consumers against products and services harmful to health.
- Protecting consumers from breach of contract by sellers.
- Ensuring supply of goods of fair quality and fair price.
- Safeguarding against misleading advertisement.
- Ensuring uninterrupted supply in correct quantity and size.
- Protecting against unfair trade practices, pollution and evil effects of competition.

tips: Dates: Consumerism 1960; CPA 1986 in force 15.4.1987; World Consumer Rights Day 15 March; Ralph Nader = father.

com.title: Rights, Duties and Responsibilities of Consumers
com.intro: To protect their interest, consumers must know their rights, and also perform their duties and responsibilities. Rights and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin.

pts: Consumer right: "the right to have information about the quality, potency, quantity, purity, price, and standard of goods or services".
**John F. Kennedy:** "The Right of Safety, the Right to be informed, the Right to choose and the Right to be heard."
Rights under CPA: Protection of health & safety, To be informed, To choose, To be heard, To seek redressal, Consumer education, Quality of life, Consumer protection, Basic needs (latest addition).

Buy quality products at reasonable price, Check weights & measures, Read labels, Beware of false advertisements, Avoid misleading schemes, Get cash bill, Buy from reputed shops, Never buy from black market, Buy standardised products (ISI), Follow manufacturer's instructions, Know consumer rights.

Pay price as per contract, take delivery in time, bear loss for delayed delivery, pay interest for delayed payment, follow instructions, state requirements clearly, collect information, get cash receipt & warranty card, file complaints, never compromise on quality (ISI, Agmark, FPO), report discrepancy in advertisements, file complaint under CPA when rights are violated.

terms: Right to get all relevant facts about a product to make intelligent decisions.
Access to the widest range of products in quality and brand at reasonable prices.
Right to get compensation within a reasonable time for genuine complaints.
Right to food, clothing, water and a pure, healthy environment.

q2.q: Write short notes on: "Right to be informed."
q2.a: Consumers should be given all relevant facts about the product so that they can take intelligent purchase decisions. The package should contain the name of the product, composition, dosage, date of manufacture, date of expiry, batch number, warnings, antidote, name of manufacturer and price with or without tax.

q2.q: What are the rights of consumer according to John F. Kennedy?
q2.a: The former US President John F. Kennedy defined the basic consumer rights as "The Right of Safety, the Right to be informed, the Right to choose and the Right to be heard."

q2.q: Which is the supreme objective of business?
q2.a: Satisfaction of consumers' wants and needs is the prime and supreme objective of a business. The modern marketing concept recognises that the consumer is the pivotal point around which the entire business moves.

q3.q: What do you understand by "Right to redressal".
q3.a:
- This right is one step ahead of the right to be heard.
- Complaints are not just to be heard; the aggrieved party is to be granted compensation within a reasonable time.
- There should be prompt, fair and just settlement of complaints and claims in a definite time frame.
- This boosts consumer confidence and renders justice to buyers.

q3.q: What do you understand about "Right to protection of health and safety".
q3.a:
- Some products may cause physical danger to consumers' health, lives and property – e.g. food additives, colours, emulsifiers, preservatives.
- These health hazards must be eradicated or reduced.
- For food items and drugs, life-saving and life-sustaining safety must be guaranteed.
- Recent legislations have shifted the responsibility for unsafe items onto sellers rather than buyers.

q3.q: Explain the right to choose and the right to be heard.
q3.a:
- **Right to choose:** Consumers should have access to the widest range of products in quality, brand, colour, design and size at reasonable prices; consumer satisfaction increases with choice.
- **Right to be heard:** Consumers can register their dissatisfaction and get the complaint heard. Every business should have a separate department for consumer grievances.

q5.q: Explain the duties of consumers. (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Buying quality products at reasonable price** after enquiring about price and quality.
2. **Ensure weights and measures** – do not buy goods weighed along with packing.
3. **Read the label carefully** for correct and complete information.
4. **Beware of false and attractive advertisements.**
5. **Avoid misleading schemes** – free gifts and discounts are already priced in.
6. **Ensure receipt of cash bill** and warranty card for seeking redressal.
7. **Buy from reputed shops** – super bazaar, cooperative stores.
8. **Never purchase from black market** or panic-buy.
9. **Buy standardised products** with quality marks.
10. **Follow the instructions of the manufacturer.**
11. **Know consumer rights** and complain when cheated.

q5.q: What are the responsibilities of consumers? (any 5)
q5.a:
1. Pay the price of goods as per the terms of the sales contract.
2. Apply for and take delivery of goods in time.
3. Bear any loss to the seller caused by delay in taking delivery.
4. Pay interest and special damages for delay in payment.
5. Follow instructions and precautions while using products.
6. Express requirements and expectations clearly to the seller.
7. Collect complete information about quality, quantity and price before purchase.
8. Get cash receipt and warranty card with date, signature and stamp of the seller.
9. File a complaint about defects with the seller.
10. Never compromise on quality – look for ISI, Agmark, FPO marks.
11. Bring discrepancy between advertised and actual features to the notice of the seller.
12. File a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 when rights are violated.

q5.q: Explain the rights of consumers.
q5.a:
1. **Right to protection of health and safety.**
2. **Right to be informed** – full details on labels.
3. **Right to choose** – widest range at reasonable prices.
4. **Right to be heard** – grievances registered and aired.
5. **Right to seek redressal** – compensation within reasonable time.
6. **Right to consumer education.**
7. **Right to quality of life** – free from pollution.
8. **Right to consumer protection** – against hazardous goods (use ISI products).
9. **Right to basic needs** – food, clothing, water, healthy environment.

tips: Kennedy's 4 rights: Safety, Informed, Choose, Heard.

com.title: Grievance Redressal Mechanism
com.intro: When consumers are cheated, they can get justice through consumer councils, the three-tier consumer courts (District Forum, State Commission, National Commission) and voluntary consumer organisations.

pts: Consumers are ignorant, illiterate, poor and not united; they are exploited by misleading ads, poor quality, short weights, overcharging.
Mahatma Gandhi: "A customer is the most important visitor on our premises..."
At District, State and Central levels – to promote and protect consumer rights.

notes.h: 18.03 Three-tier courts (pecuniary jurisdiction as per book)

**State Commission** – above ₹20 lakhs up to ₹1 crore; President: a High Court Judge; 2 members (one woman). Appeals from District Forum.
**National Commission (NCDRC)** – above ₹1 crore; set up 1988; New Delhi; headed by a serving/retired Supreme Court Judge; 5 members including a woman. Section 21.
Appeals: District → State → National → Supreme Court, each **within 30 days**.
More than 620 District Forums and 30 State Commissions. Helpline 1800-11-4000 / 14404.

Within **2 years**; no stamp paper; no advocate needed.

Consumer Welfare Fund (CWF) by Department of Consumer Affairs.
Functions: awareness, testing products, filing suits for consumers, protests against adulteration, helping educational institutions, networking, supporting government.
IOCU established **1960**, London.

q2.q: What do you meant by Redressal Mechanism?
q2.a: Redressal mechanism is the arrangement for settling the grievances of consumers who are exploited through misleading advertisements, poor quality goods, short weights and overcharging. Under the Consumer Protection Act, it consists of Consumer Councils and the three-tier courts – District Forum, State Commission and National Commission.

q2.q: What do you know about National Commission?
q2.a: The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) is a quasi-judicial commission set up in 1988 under the Consumer Protection Act 1986, with its head office in New Delhi. It is headed by a serving or retired judge of the Supreme Court and entertains complaints valued above ₹1 crore.

q2.q: State the meaning of the term State Commission.
q2.a: The State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is appointed by the State Government. It is headed by a High Court judge and entertains complaints above ₹20 lakhs up to ₹1 crore and appeals against District Forum orders.

q2.q: What is an term District Forum?
q2.a: As per Section 9 of the Consumer Protection Act 1986, the State Government establishes a District Forum in each district to protect aggrieved consumers. It is headed by a District Judge and entertains complaints where the value is up to ₹20 lakhs.

q3.q: Who are the members of the National Commission?
q3.a:
- The National Commission should have five members.
- One should be from the judiciary – a serving or retired Supreme Court judge as President.
- Four other members of ability, knowledge and experience from other fields.
- It should include a woman.

q3.q: Who are the members of the State Commission?
q3.a:
- A person who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, appointed by the State Government, as its President.
- Two other members of ability, integrity and standing with knowledge of economics, law, commerce, industry, public affairs or administration.
- One of them shall be a woman.

q3.q: Write a note on the Voluntary Consumer Organisation.
q3.a:
- Voluntary consumer organisations are formed voluntarily by consumers to protect their rights and interests.
- The Department of Consumer Affairs operates the Consumer Welfare Fund (CWF) to strengthen the consumer movement and supports VCOs with grants.
- They create awareness (brochures, seminars), test products and publish results, file suits on behalf of consumers, organise protests against adulteration and hoarding, and support the government.

q3.q: Who are the members of the District Forum?
q3.a:
- A person who is or has been or is qualified to be a District Judge as its President.
- Two other members of ability, integrity and standing with knowledge of economics, law, commerce, accountancy, industry or administration.
- One of the two members shall be a woman.

q5.q: Explain the overall performance of National Commission.
q5.a:
- **Set up:** 1988 under CPA 1986; head office New Delhi; headed by a serving or retired Supreme Court judge.
- **Members:** five members – one from judiciary, four from other fields, including a woman.
- **Jurisdiction (Section 21):** (1) complaints valued above ₹1 crore (2) revising orders of State Commissions (3) calling for records and passing orders from State Commissions and District Forums.
- **Powers:** uniform procedure in hearings; prior service of copies of documents to opposite parties; speedy grant of copies; overseeing State Commissions and District Forums without interfering with their quasi-judicial freedom.
- **Appellate:** acts where a State Commission exceeded or failed to exercise jurisdiction; under Section 23, appeal against National Commission orders lies to the Supreme Court within 30 days.

q5.q: Explain the overall performance of State Commission.
q5.a:
- **Appointment:** by State Government in consultation with the Centre; also called Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission; covers goods and services.
- **Members:** a present/former High Court Judge as President and two other members, one of whom shall be a woman.
- **Jurisdiction:** (1) complaints within the state where value exceeds ₹20 lakhs and is below ₹1 crore (2) appeals against orders of District Forums.
- **Powers:** call for records and pass orders in disputes pending or decided by District Forums; require production of books of accounts, documents or commodities; obtain information.
- **Appellate:** jurisdiction may be original, appellate or revision; may confirm or reverse District Forum orders; appeal against its order lies to the National Commission within 30 days.

q5.q: Explain the procedure for filing a consumer complaint.
q5.a:
- **First step:** send a legal notice to the seller with consumer details, problem, action expected and time given.
- **Who can complain:** consumer, registered VCO, Central Govt, State Govt/UT, consumers with same interest.
- **When:** unfair trade practice, defective goods, deficient services, excess price, hazardous goods.
- **How:** within 2 years; no stamp paper; in person, by agent or by post; no advocate needed.
- **Particulars:** names and addresses, date of purchase, amount paid, details of complaint, bills and receipts.
- **Reliefs:** remove defects, replace goods, refund price, compensation, discontinue unfair trade practice, withdraw hazardous goods, costs.

tips: Draw the three-tier pyramid: District (≤₹20 lakh) → State (₹20 lakh–₹1 crore) → National (>₹1 crore). Appeal within 30 days at each level.

com.title: Environmental Factors
com.intro: Business environment is the sum total of all internal and external factors that affect a business. This chapter covers internal, micro and macro environment, VUCA, corporate governance and GST.

pts: **Bayard O. Wheeler:** Business environment is "the total of all things external to firms and industries which affect their organisation and operations".
Internal environment (controllable) → Strengths & Weaknesses. External (uncontrollable) → Opportunities & Threats (SWOT).
Significance: strategy & planning, identifying opportunities (Apollo Hospitals), environment scanning for threats (Fuji Films vs digital cameras), business aids, public image (More home delivery).
Value system, Vision & objectives (Amul), Management structure, Internal power relations, Human resources, Company image, Other factors (R&D, capital, marketing, physical assets).
Financiers, Suppliers, Marketing channel members, Public (e.g. Sterlite Copper closure 2018), Customers, Competitors.
Economic, Socio-cultural, Political & legal, Geo-physical, Technological, Global.
**Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity** – developed in late 1980s by the US military.
Rules and policies that govern a company. Four pillars: **fairness, transparency, accountability, responsibility**.
Committees: Kumara Mangalam Birla (2000), Narayana Murthy (2003), Adi Godrej (2008), Uday Kotak.
Listed companies: ≥ 1/3 independent directors, at least one independent woman director, disclose related party deals and managerial compensation, CEO & CFO certification.
Comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based indirect tax on every value addition.
**CGST** (Centre, intra-state), **SGST** (State, intra-state), **IGST** (Centre, inter-state).
GST Council – chaired by the Union Finance Minister.

terms: Sum total of all internal and external factors affecting a business.
Factors within an organisation that are controllable.
Immediate environment – financiers, suppliers, channel members, public, customers, competitors.
General environment – economic, social, political, geo-physical, technological, global (uncontrollable).
Set of rules and policies which governs a company.
Goods and Services Tax – destination-based indirect tax on every value addition.

q2.a: Internal environment refers to the factors within an organisation, e.g. policies and programmes, organisational structure, employees, financial and physical resources. These factors can be changed or altered and hence are known as controllable factors.

q2.q: Give the meaning of corporate governance.
q2.a: Corporate governance is a set of rules and policies which governs a company. It provides a framework for managing a company and achieving its objectives, and gives guidelines for internal control, performance measurement and corporate disclosure. It is based on fairness, transparency, accountability and responsibility.

GST is the indirect tax levied on goods and services across the country. It is a comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based tax levied on every value addition. It has three components – CGST, SGST and IGST.
VUCA – Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity and Ambiguity. It was developed in the late 80s by the U.S. military.

q3.q: What are the political environment factors? (any 3)
q3.a:
- **Political stability:** election system, law and order, role of military and police, President's rule, civil war.
- **Political organisation:** ideology of political parties, authority of bureaucracy, political consciousness, funding of parties.
- Image of the leader and the country in the international arena.
- Legal framework of business and its flexibility.
- The constitution of the nation.
- Foreign policy with reference to tariffs and free trade.

q3.q: Write about any three internal environmental factors of business.
q3.a:
- **Value system:** values of the founder percolate to the whole organisation; strong ethical culture attracts business associates.
- **Vision and objectives:** guide operations and strategic decisions, e.g. Amul.
- **Management structure and nature:** composition and professionalism of the board affect decision making.
- **Human resources:** quality, skill, attitude and commitment of manpower decide success.
- **Company image:** helps in launching products, raising finance, entering new markets.

q3.q: What do you know about Technological environment?
q3.a:
- Developments in IT and telecommunication have created a global market.
- Technology is used in market research, digital and social media advertising, data mining and analytics, inventory management, warehousing, distribution and payments.
- It includes the level of technology in the country, rate of change in technology, technology adopted by competitors and technological obsolescence.

q5.q: Discuss the role of macro environment of business. (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Economic environment:** nature of economy (developed/developing/under-developed), economic system (capitalistic, socialistic, mixed), economic policies (monetary, fiscal, EXIM, industrial), economic indices (GDP, GNP, per capita income), development of financial markets and economic structure.
2. **Socio-cultural environment:** social institutions, family structure, marriage, caste, customs and beliefs, demographic factors, lifestyle and tastes.
3. **Political and legal environment:** political stability, political organisation, image of the leader, legal framework, constitution, foreign policy.
4. **Geo-physical environment:** natural resources, weather and climate, topography, ecological factors (plastic ban in Ooty), location of industries (textiles in Coimbatore), harbours and ports.
5. **Technological environment:** level and rate of change of technology, competitors' technology, obsolescence.
6. **Global environment:** differences in language, culture, currencies, norms, tastes, tax structure and technology adoption.

q5.q: Explain the micro environmental factors of business. (any 5)
q5.a:
1. **Financiers:** debenture holders and financial institutions – their financial capability, policies and attitude to risk.
2. **Suppliers:** timely supply of raw materials ensures continuity of production and lower inventory cost; firms keep a panel of suppliers.
3. **Marketing channel members:** dealers, wholesalers, retailers, transporters, warehouses, market research and advertising agencies, insurance firms.
4. **Public:** media groups, citizen action groups, local public can make or mar a business (e.g. Sterlite Copper, Thoothukudi, 2018).
5. **Customers:** the king and fulcrum of business; CRM builds cordial relations.
6. **Competitors:** at local, national and global levels; firms modify strategies to face them.

q5.q: Explain the corporate governance framework in India.
q5.a:
- Corporate governance is a set of rules and policies which governs a company; four pillars – fairness, transparency, accountability, responsibility.
- Committees: Kumara Mangalam Birla 2000, Narayana Murthy 2003, Adi Godrej 2008, Uday Kotak.
- Norms in Companies Act 2013, SEBI listing regulations and Clause 49.
- Listed companies must have at least one-third independent directors, at least one independent woman director, disclose related party deals and managerial compensation; CEO and CFO must certify compliance.
- It enhances image, increases investor confidence and safeguards shareholders.

tips: Internal = controllable; External (micro + macro) = uncontrollable.

com.title: Liberalization, Privatization and Globalization
com.intro: In 1991 India adopted the New Economic Policy (NEP) – Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation (LPG) – after receiving loans from the World Bank and IMF. This chapter covers the meaning, forms, advantages, disadvantages and impact of each.

pts: Three dimensions: Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation.
Base: **Dunkel Draft** (GATT) by Arthur Dunkel – 22,000 page document for WTO.
Dr. Manmohan Singh – architect of Indian economic reforms (1991).
Relaxation of government restrictions; abolished "Licence Raj".
Forms: industrial licensing relaxed (6 industries kept, now 5), freedom of production, SSI investment limit ₹1 crore, foreign exchange reforms (rupee devalued 1991), EXIM liberalisation.
Advantages: foreign investment, forex reserves, consumption, price control, less external borrowing.
Disadvantages: unemployment, loss to domestic units, dependence on foreign nations, unbalanced development.
Transferring ownership from government to private sector. First privatised: India Scooters Ltd. Others: BALCO, HZL, IPCL, Maruti Udyog, Modern Food Industries.
Forms: contraction of public sector (17 → 8 → now Atomic Energy, Defence, Railways), sale of PSU shares, MoU system (1991), disinvestment.
Advantages: efficiency, professional management, competition, less burden on govt. Disadvantages: lack of welfare, political pressure, ignores weaker sections.
Integration of the domestic economy with the rest of the world.
Forms: foreign trade policy (TRIPS, GATS), export promotion, freedom to repatriate, reduction in tariffs, open competition.
Advantages: foreign collaboration, market expansion, technology, reduced brain drain. Disadvantages: loss of domestic industries, inequalities, dominance of foreign institutions.
New foreign trade agreements, FDI & FII, MRTP Act amended, deregulation, overseas trade, inflation control, tax reforms, abolition of licence.

terms: Relaxation of government restrictions in social and economic policies.
Transfer of ownership of enterprises from government to private sector.
Integration of the domestic economy with the world economy.
Selling government stake in PSUs to the private sector.
Loss of educated and talented workers to other countries through migration.
To send or bring money back to one's own country.

q2.q: State the branches of New Economic Policy.
q2.a:
The three dimensions (branches) of the New Economic Policy are:
- Liberalisation
- Privatisation
- Globalisation

Privatisation is the process of transferring ownership of a business enterprise, agency or public service from the government to the private sector. It means permitting the private sector to set up industries which were previously reserved for the public sector.

q2.q: Mention any two disadvantages of Liberalisation.
q2.a:
- **Increase in unemployment:** some industries decline and close, causing structural unemployment.
- **Loss to domestic units:** new entrants pose threat and competition to existing domestic units.

q2.q: Give any two advantages of Globalisation.
q2.a:
- **Increase in foreign collaboration** through joint ventures, mergers, franchises, turn-key projects.
- **Expansion of market** from local to national to international.

q3.q: What do you mean by Liberalisation?
q3.a:
- Liberalisation means relaxation of various government restrictions in the areas of social and economic policies so that economies are free to enter the market and establish ventures.
- It includes removal of tariffs, subsidies and other restrictions on flow of goods and services between countries.
- It is the result of the New Industrial Policy which abolished the "Licence Raj".

q3.q: State any three impacts on Globalisation.
q3.a:
- Corporations got competitive advantage from lower operating costs and access to new raw materials and markets.
- MNCs can manufacture, buy and sell goods worldwide.
- Boom in consumer products market.
- Job creation due to foreign companies and economic growth.
- Technological advancement in agriculture.

q3.q: Write a short note on New Economic Policy.
q3.a:
- In 1991 India approached the World Bank (IBRD) and IMF for loans to repay external borrowings.
- They expected India to liberalise and open up the economy.
- India announced the New Economic Policy with wide-ranging reforms known as LPG – Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation.
- Its base is the Dunkel Draft of GATT submitted by Arthur Dunkel for the WTO.

q5.q: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of liberalisation. (any 5)
q5.a:
**Advantages**
1. **Increase in foreign investment** – capital inflows, technology, management techniques.
2. **Increase in foreign exchange reserve** – easy access to foreign capital.
3. **Increase in consumption** – more goods available.
4. **Control over price** – removal of tariffs lowers prices.
5. **Reduction in external borrowings.**
**Disadvantages**
1. **Increase in unemployment** – structural unemployment from closure of some industries.
2. **Loss to domestic units** – competition from new entrants.
3. **Increased dependence on foreign nations** – domination by big institutions.
4. **Unbalanced development** – benefits developed rather than developing countries.

q5.q: What are the highlights of the LPG policy? (any 5)
q5.a:
1. Introduction of new Foreign Trade Agreements.
2. Foreign Investment (FDI and FII).
3. MRTP Act, 1969 amended.
4. Deregulation.
5. Opportunities for overseas trade.
6. Steps to regulate inflation.
7. Tax reforms.
8. Abolition of Licence.

q5.q: Explain the forms of privatisation.
q5.a:
1. **Contraction of public sector:** industries reserved for public sector reduced from 17 (1956) to 8; now only Atomic Energy, Defence and Railways.
2. **Sale of shares of PSUs** to the public and financial institutions; private share rose from 45% to 55% by 2011.
3. **Memorandum of Understanding (1991):** to raise productivity and judge PSU performance.
4. **Disinvestment** in loss-making PSUs – selling them to the private sector.

q5.q: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of globalisation.
q5.a:
**Advantages:** increase in foreign collaboration; expansion of market; technological development; reduction in brain drain.
**Disadvantages:** loss of domestic industries; increase in inequalities between rich and poor; dominance of foreign institutions threatening national sovereignty.

tips: 1991 is the key year: NEP, rupee devaluation, MoU system.

com.title: The Sale of Goods Act, 1930
com.unit: Unit VIII – Sale of Goods Act & Negotiable Instruments Act
com.intro: The Sale of Goods Act was passed in 1930 (earlier it was Chapter 7 of the Indian Contract Act 1872). It covers the contract of sale, sale vs agreement to sell, types of goods, transfer of ownership, conditions and warranties, and rights of an unpaid seller.

pts: A contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property (ownership) in goods to the buyer for a price.
**Essential elements:** Two parties, Transfer of property, Goods, Price, Includes both sale and agreement to sell.
Goods exclude money, actionable claims and immovable property; include stocks & shares, growing crops, goodwill, trademarks, copyrights, patents, water, gas, electricity.
Goods for goods = barter, not sale.
Sale: ownership passes immediately (executed contract). Agreement to sell: ownership passes at a future date or after conditions (executory contract).
**Existing goods:** Specific, Ascertained, Unascertained (generic).
**Future goods:** to be manufactured/acquired after the contract.
**Contingent goods:** acquisition depends on a contingency (part of future goods).
Specific goods – at the time of contract (deliverable state) or later (when made deliverable / weighed / tested).
Unascertained goods – when ascertained, appropriated (bilateral) or delivered to carrier.
Goods on approval / sale or return – on approval, on adoption, or on expiry of time.
**Condition:** essential to the main purpose; breach → cancel contract + damages.
**Warranty:** collateral; breach → damages only.
**Implied conditions:** Title, Description, Sale by sample, Quality or fitness, Merchantability, Wholesomeness, Trade usage.
**Implied warranties:** Quiet possession, Free from encumbrances, Dangerous goods (warn the buyer).
Whole price not paid, or bill/cheque dishonoured.
**Against goods:** Lien, Stoppage in transit, Resale (and withholding delivery where ownership has not passed).
**Against buyer personally:** Suit for price, Suit for damages for non-acceptance, Suit for cancellation before due date, Suit for interest.

terms: Seller transfers or agrees to transfer ownership of goods to buyer for a price.
Every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money.
Goods identified and agreed upon at the time of contract.
Goods to be manufactured, produced or acquired after the contract.
Goods whose acquisition depends on an uncertain event.
Stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract.
Stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract.
Seller who has not received the whole price or whose cheque/bill is dishonoured.
Right of unpaid seller to retain goods in his possession till price is paid.

mcq.q: Sale of Goods Act was passed in the year
Which of the below constitutes the essential element of contract of sale?
Which of the below is not a good?
In case of the sale, the ____ has the right to sell
The property in the goods means the
Breach of warranty entitles the affected party to
Exchange of goods for goods is called
A sale is an ______ contract.

q2.q: What is a contract of sale of goods?
q2.a: Contract of sale of goods is a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property (ownership) of the goods to the buyer for a price. It includes both sale and agreement to sell.

q2.q: List down the essential elements of a contract of sale.
q2.a:
- Two parties – seller and buyer
- Transfer of property (ownership)
- Goods as subject matter
- Price (money consideration)
- Includes both sale and agreement to sell

Goods mean every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money. It includes stocks, shares, growing crops, grass, things attached to land agreed to be cut before sale, goodwill, copyright, trademark, patents, water, gas, electricity and power.

Contingent goods are goods whose acquisition by the seller depends upon a contingency (an event which may or may not happen). They are a part of future goods. E.g. a rice merchant agrees to supply 10 bags of basmati rice from Pakistan if he gets supplies.

q3.q: Discuss in detail about existing goods.
q3.a:
Existing goods are those owned or possessed by the seller at the time of contract of sale. They may be:
- **Specific goods:** identified and agreed upon at the time of contract, e.g. a saree selected after examining several sarees.
- **Ascertained goods:** similar to specific goods; also goods which become ascertained after the formation of the contract.
- **Unascertained or generic goods:** not identified and agreed upon at the time of contract, e.g. the various car models displayed in a showroom.

q3.q: Discuss the implied conditions and warranties in sale of goods contract.
q3.a:
**Implied conditions**
- Condition as to title – seller has the right to sell.
- Condition as to description – goods must agree with the description.
- Sale by sample – bulk must correspond with the sample.
- Quality or fitness for the purpose made known to the seller.
- Merchantability – goods must be saleable under that name.
- Wholesomeness – eatables must be fit for consumption.
- Condition implied by trade usage.
**Implied warranties**
- Quiet possession of the goods.
- Goods free from any encumbrance.
- Warning about dangerous goods.

q3.q: Distinguish between sale and agreement to sell.
q3.a:
| Basis | Sale | Agreement to Sell |
| Ownership | Passes to buyer immediately | Passes at a future date or after conditions |
| Risk of loss | Falls on the buyer | Falls on the seller |
| Buyer fails to pay | Seller can only sue for price | Seller can repossess goods and sue for damages |
| Nature | Executed contract | Executory contract |
| Buyer insolvent | Seller must hand over goods to Official Receiver | Seller can retain goods |
| Seller insolvent | Buyer can claim goods | Buyer gets only rateable dividend |

q5.q: Explain in detail the elements of Contract of sale.
q5.a:
1. **Two parties:** seller and buyer must be different persons. A person cannot buy his own goods (except buying his goods sold in execution of a decree). Distribution of assets among partners on dissolution is not a sale.
2. **Transfer of property:** the seller must transfer or agree to transfer ownership; mere transfer of possession is not a sale.
3. **Goods:** subject matter must be goods – movable property including stocks, shares, growing crops, goodwill, trademarks, copyrights, patents; excludes money, actionable claims and immovable property.
4. **Price:** money consideration. Goods for goods is barter; goods partly for goods and partly for money is a sale.
5. **Includes sale and agreement to sell:** if ownership passes immediately it is a sale; if at a future date or on fulfilment of conditions it is an agreement to sell.

q5.q: Distinguish between Conditions and Warranty.
q5.a:
| Basis | Condition | Warranty |
| Meaning | Stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract | Stipulation collateral to the main purpose |
| Significance | So essential that its breach cancels the contract | Subsidiary; breach does not revoke the contract |
| Transfer of ownership | Cannot be transferred without fulfilling conditions | Can be transferred without fulfilling warranty |
| Remedy | Cancel the contract and claim damages | Claim damages only |
| Treatment | Breach of condition may be treated as breach of warranty | Breach of warranty cannot be treated as breach of condition |
Example: A wants a bike giving 50 km/litre (condition) in red colour (warranty). B supplies a green bike giving 55 km/litre – A cannot cancel, but can make B bear the cost of repainting.

q5.q: Explain the rights of an unpaid seller.
q5.a:
**I. Against the goods**
1. **Right of lien:** retain goods in his possession till price is paid (goods sold without credit, or credit expired, or buyer insolvent). Lost when goods are delivered to a carrier without reserving disposal, buyer obtains possession, or seller waives it.
2. **Right of stoppage in transit:** when goods are with a carrier and the buyer becomes insolvent, the seller can stop and regain them. Ends when goods are delivered to buyer or carrier acknowledges holding them for the buyer.
3. **Right of resale:** for perishable goods, after lien/stoppage if buyer does not pay within reasonable time after notice, or when expressly reserved.
4. Where ownership has not passed – withholding delivery.
**II. Against the buyer personally**
1. Suit for price.
2. Suit for damages for non-acceptance.
3. Suit for cancellation of the contract before the due date.
4. Suit for interest.

tips: Condition vs Warranty with the bike example is a sure-shot 5-mark question.

com.title: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
com.unit: Unit VIII – Sale of Goods Act & Negotiable Instruments Act
com.intro: A negotiable instrument is a document entitling a person to a sum of money, transferable by delivery or by endorsement and delivery. This chapter covers promissory notes, bills of exchange, cheques, their comparison, crossing of cheques and endorsements.

pts: 'Negotiable' = transferable for consideration; 'Instrument' = written document creating a right.

**Justice K.C. Willis:** "a negotiable instrument is one, the property in which is acquired by anyone who takes it bonafide and for value, notwithstanding any defect to title in the person from whom he took it."
**Section 13:** a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer.
Characteristics: Transferability, Title of holder in due course free from defects, Right of transferee to sue in own name.
8 presumptions: consideration, acceptance, date, acceptance before maturity, transfer before maturity, order of endorsements, stamp, holder in due course.
Negotiability: by delivery/endorsement; no notice needed; better title; consideration presumed.
Assignability: formalities (writing, stamp); notice needed; title subject to defects; consideration must be proved.
**Promissory Note (Sec 4):** unconditional undertaking signed by the maker to pay a certain sum – 2 parties (maker, payee). Cannot be payable to bearer.
**Bill of Exchange (Sec 5):** unconditional order signed by the maker directing a certain person to pay – 3 parties (drawer, drawee, payee). 3 days of grace.
**Cheque (Sec 6):** a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand. Stale after 3 months.
**General crossing (Sec 123):** two parallel transverse lines with or without "& Co." – paid only through a banker.
**Special crossing (Sec 124):** name of a banker added – paid only to that banker. Safer.
Signing on the back (or face) for negotiation. Extra paper attached = **Allonge**.
Kinds: Blank/general, Full/special, Conditional, Restrictive, Sans recourse, Facultative, Partial (invalid).
MICR – Magnetic Ink Character Recognition; IFSC – 11-character code (4 letters bank + 0 + 6 branch).

terms: Promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable to order or bearer.
Person who takes the instrument in good faith and for value.
Unconditional undertaking signed by the maker to pay a certain sum of money.
Unconditional order directing a certain person to pay a certain sum.
Bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker payable on demand.
Two parallel transverse lines on a cheque so that it is paid only through a bank.
Signing on the instrument to transfer one's interest in it.
Slip of paper attached to an instrument for further endorsements.
