q2.a: The capital of a company is divided into small units of fixed amount. These units are called shares. Shares are of two types – preference shares and equity shares.

When the number of shares applied for is more than the number of shares offered for subscription, it is said to be over subscription. It is dealt with by rejecting some applications fully, by pro rata allotment, or by a combination of both.

q2.q: What is meant by calls in arrear?
q2.a: When a shareholder fails to pay the amount due on allotment or on calls, the amount remaining unpaid is known as calls in arrear, i.e., the amount called up but not paid. As per Table F, interest not exceeding 10% p.a. may be charged on it if the Articles so provide.

q2.q: Write a short note on securities premium account.
q2.a: When a company issues shares at a price more than the face value, the excess is called premium and is transferred to securities premium account. Premium may be collected with application, allotment or a call. It is shown under reserves and surplus as a separate head in the Note to Accounts to the balance sheet.

When a shareholder defaults in making payment of allotment and/or call money, the shares may be forfeited. On forfeiture, the share allotment is cancelled, share capital is reduced to that extent and the person ceases to be a shareholder. The amount already paid is forfeited and is a gain to the company.

q3.q: State the differences between preference shares and equity shares.
q3.a:
| Basis | Preference shares | Equity shares |
| Preference for dividend | Preferential right to dividend | No preferential right |
| Rate of dividend | Fixed rate | Not fixed; depends on profits |
| Repayment of capital on winding up | Paid before equity shareholders | Paid after preference shareholders |
| Other name | – | Ordinary shares |

q3.q: Write a brief note on calls in advance.
q3.a:
- The excess amount paid over the called up value of a share is known as calls in advance (excess paid on application, allotment or calls).
- It may be returned or adjusted towards future payments and may be transferred to a separate calls in advance account.
- It does not form part of share capital and no dividend is payable on it; it is shown under **current liabilities**.
- Sec 50: accepted only if authorised by the Articles. Table F: interest up to **12% p.a.** may be paid.
- Entries: Bank A/c Dr – To Calls in advance A/c; later Calls in advance A/c Dr – To Share call A/c.

q3.q: What is reissue of forfeited shares?
q3.a:
- Shares forfeited can be reissued by the company at any price, but the reissue price cannot be less than the amount unpaid on forfeited shares (e.g. ₹10 share with ₹4 paid – minimum ₹6).
- Loss on reissue is debited to forfeited shares account; premium on reissue is credited to securities premium account.
- Entry: Bank A/c Dr, Forfeited shares A/c Dr (loss) – To Share capital A/c.
- The remaining gain on reissued shares is capital profit: Forfeited shares A/c Dr – To Capital reserve A/c (proportionate if only part reissued).

q3.q: Write a short note on (a) Authorised capital (b) Reserve capital
q3.a:
- **(a) Authorised capital:** such capital as is authorised by the memorandum of association. It is the maximum amount which can be raised as capital. Also called registered capital or nominal capital.
- **(b) Reserve capital:** the company can reserve a part of its subscribed capital to be called up only at the time of winding up. It is called reserve capital.

q3.q: What is meant by issue of shares for consideration other than cash?
q3.a:
- A company may issue shares for consideration other than cash when it acquires fixed assets such as land, buildings or machinery, or purchases a business, or to promoters for services and to brokers/underwriters for commission.
- Entries: Asset A/c Dr – To Vendor A/c (purchase); Vendor A/c Dr – To Equity share capital A/c and To Securities premium A/c (if at premium).
- Number of shares = Amount payable ÷ Issue price.

tips: Forfeiture: debit capital with CALLED-UP amount, never face value (unless fully called).
Debit securities premium on forfeiture only when premium has not been received.
Capital reserve = amount forfeited on reissued shares – loss on reissue.

acc.title: Financial Statement Analysis
acc.intro: Financial statements tell us totals; analysis tells us what they mean. This unit covers the meaning, features, significance and limitations of financial statements, objectives of analysis, and three tools you must be able to work: comparative statements, common-size statements and trend percentages.

pts: Statements prepared at the end of the accounting period to ascertain **operating results** and **financial position** – the **income statement** and the **balance sheet** (also cash flow, funds flow statements).

Features: prepared at the end of the period from recorded transactions; for the organisation as a whole; grouped items (fixed / current); **historical cost**; follow accounting principles & standards; involve personal judgement.

Management – decisions and control; Shareholders – growth potential; Potential investors – value securities; Creditors – ability to repay; Bankers – security for loans; Government – tax and industrial policy; Employees – ability to pay salaries and future growth.
Lack of qualitative information; record of historical data; ignore price level changes; lack of consistency; only interim reports; limited access to external users; influenced by personal judgement.
**Sec 2(40):** balance sheet, P&L / I&E account, cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity and explanatory notes.
**Sec 129(1):** true and fair view, comply with Accounting Standards (Sec 133), in the form of **Schedule III**.
Comparison of items by establishing and evaluating relationships among them – includes **analysis** (examination & comparison) and **interpretation** (explanation of results).

Objectives: profitability; long- and short-term solvency; operating efficiency; efficiency of management; trends; forecasting/budgets; **inter-firm** (with other firms) and **intra-firm** (within departments) comparison.
Limitations: limitations of financial statements apply; only a means not an end; needs expert knowledge; involves personal judgement.
**Comparative statement** – compares items for two or more years: absolute change and percentage change.
**Common-size statement** – items as % of a common base (revenue from operations = 100; balance sheet total = 100).
**Trend analysis** – base year = 100; other years as % of base; used for **more than two years**.
**Funds flow analysis** – fund = **working capital** (current assets – current liabilities); sources and applications.
**Cash flow analysis** – inflow and outflow of cash and cash equivalents; assesses liquidity and solvency.
**Horizontal analysis** – several years (comparative, trend). **Vertical analysis** – one year (common-size, ratios).

terms: Statements prepared at the end of the accounting period to ascertain operating results and financial position.

q2.a: Financial statements are the statements prepared by business concerns at the end of the accounting period to ascertain the operating results and the financial position. The basic financial statements are the income statement (showing net results for a period) and the balance sheet (showing financial position as on a date).

q2.q: List the tools of financial statement analysis.
q2.a: (i) Comparative statement (ii) Common-size statement (iii) Trend analysis (iv) Funds flow analysis (v) Cash flow analysis.
Working capital refers to the excess of current assets over current liabilities. The term 'fund' in funds flow analysis refers to working capital.

q2.q: When is trend analysis preferred to other tools?
q2.a: When data for more than two years are to be analysed, it may be difficult to use comparative statement. In such cases trend analysis is used, taking the first year as base year (100) and expressing other years' figures as a percentage of it.

q3.q: 'Financial statements are prepared based on the past data'. Explain how this is a limitation.
q3.a:
- Financial statements are prepared based on **historical data** (historical cost).
- Hence they may **not reflect the current position** of the business.
- Adjustments for **price level changes** are not made, so values of assets may differ from current values and the statements may not reveal the current financial position or be useful for future decisions.

q3.q: Write a short note on cash flow analysis.
q3.a:
- Cash flow analysis is concerned with preparation of a **cash flow statement** which shows the **inflow and outflow of cash and cash equivalents** in a given period of time.
- Cash includes cash in hand and demand deposits with banks.
- Cash equivalents denote short-term investments which can be realised easily within a short period without much loss in value.
- It helps in assessing the **liquidity and solvency** of a business concern.

q3.q: Briefly explain any three limitations of financial statements.
q3.a:
1. **Lack of qualitative information:** non-monetary information such as efficiency of employees and management is ignored.
2. **Record of historical data:** prepared on historical data; may not reflect the current position.
3. **Ignore price level changes:** no adjustment is made for price changes, so the current position may not be revealed.
(Also: lack of consistency, interim reports only, limited access to external users, influenced by personal judgement.)

q3.q: Explain the steps involved in preparing comparative statement.
q3.a:
A comparative statement has five columns:
1. **Column 1:** particulars of items of income statement or balance sheet.
2. **Column 2:** absolute amount of year 1.
3. **Column 3:** absolute amount of year 2.
4. **Column 4:** difference between year 1 and year 2 – plus sign for increase, minus for decrease.
5. **Column 5:** percentage increase/decrease = Column 4 ÷ Column 2 × 100.

q3.q: Explain the procedure for preparing common-size statement.
q3.a:
A common-size statement has three columns:
1. **Column 1:** particulars of items of income statement or balance sheet.
2. **Column 2:** absolute amounts.
3. **Column 3:** choose a common base as 100 – revenue from operations for income statement and total of balance sheet for balance sheet – and work out the percentage of every item in terms of the common base.

tips: Comparative % is always on YEAR 1 (old) figure, not the new one.
Common-size: income statement base = revenue from operations; balance sheet base = total.
Show + and – signs clearly; examiners award marks for signs.
Tax is computed on profit before tax of that year, then included in the statement.

pts: Particulars | Year 1 | Year 2 | Absolute change (Year 2 – Year 1) | % change
% change = Absolute increase or decrease ÷ Year 1 amount × 100
Income statement: % = Item ÷ Revenue from operations × 100
Balance sheet: % = Item ÷ Total assets (or Total equity & liabilities) × 100
Trend % = Current year amount ÷ Base year amount × 100 (base year = 100)
| Line | Item |
| 1 | Revenue from operations |
| 2 | Add: Other income → Total revenue |
| 3 | Less: Expenses → Profit before tax |

acc.title: Ratio Analysis
acc.intro: Ratio analysis is the most powerful tool to judge a business – its liquidity, long-term solvency, efficiency and profitability. Learn each formula with its components and you can score full marks in this unit; numerical questions are direct.

pts: **Ratio** = mathematical expression of relationship between two related items. Ratios based on accounting information = **accounting ratios**.
Forms: **pure** (2:1), **percentage** (25%), **times** (4 times).
Tool of financial statement analysis by calculating ratios. **Myers:** "Ratio analysis is a study of relationship among various financial factors in a business".
Simplify accounting figures; facilitate analysis; analyse operational efficiency; help budgeting and forecasting; facilitate intra-firm and inter-firm comparison.
**Traditional:** balance sheet ratios (both items from balance sheet), income statement ratios, inter-statement ratios (one from each).
**Functional (most used):** liquidity, long-term solvency, turnover, profitability.
**Current ratio** = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities (ideal **2:1**).
**Quick (liquid / acid test) ratio** = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities (ideal **1:1**); Quick assets = CA – Inventories – Prepaid expenses.
Current assets: current investments, inventories, trade receivables (net of provision), cash & cash equivalents, short-term loans & advances, other current assets (prepaid, accrued).
Current liabilities: short-term borrowings, trade payables (creditors + B/P), other current liabilities (expenses payable, income received in advance), short-term provisions.
Very high current ratio may mean inefficient investment policy.
**Debt equity ratio** = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds (1:1 satisfactory; lower = less risk).
Shareholders' funds = Equity share capital + Preference share capital + Reserves & surplus (= Total assets – Non-current liabilities – Current liabilities). Debit balance of P&L is negative.
**Proprietary ratio** = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets (higher = less dependence on outsiders).

**Capital gearing ratio** = Funds bearing fixed interest/dividend (preference capital + debentures + fixed-interest loans) ÷ Equity shareholders' funds (equity capital + reserves). >1 = **highly geared**.
**Inventory turnover** = Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory.
**Trade receivables turnover** = Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables (debtors + B/R).
**Trade payables turnover** = Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables (creditors + B/P).
**Fixed assets turnover** = Revenue from operations ÷ Average fixed assets.
If opening figure not given, use closing figure.
**Gross profit ratio**, **Operating cost ratio**, **Operating profit ratio**, **Net profit ratio**, **Return on investment**.
Operating cost excludes non-operating items (e.g. loss on sale of fixed assets, finance cost).
Operating cost ratio + Operating profit ratio = 100%.
Measuring operational efficiency; measuring financial solvency; facilitating investment decisions; analysing profitability; intra-firm comparison; inter-firm comparison.
Ratios are only means; accuracy depends on financial information; needs consistency in preparation; non-availability of standards/norms; ignore price level changes.

q2.q: What is meant by accounting ratios?
q2.a: Ratio is a mathematical expression of relationship between two related or interdependent items, calculated by dividing one item by the other. When ratios are calculated on the basis of accounting information, they are called accounting ratios. They may be expressed as pure ratio (2:1), percentage (25%) or times (4 times).

Quick ratio gives the proportion of quick assets to current liabilities. It indicates whether the business is in a position to pay its current liabilities out of quick assets. Quick assets = Current assets – Inventories – Prepaid expenses. It is also called liquid ratio or acid test ratio. Quick ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities.

q2.q: What is meant by debt equity ratio?
q2.a: Debt equity ratio expresses the relationship between long-term debt and shareholders' funds. It is calculated to assess the long-term solvency of a business. Debt equity ratio = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds.

q2.q: What does return on investment ratio indicate?
q2.a: Return on investment shows the proportion of net profit before interest and tax to capital employed. It measures how efficiently the capital employed is used in the business and is an overall measure of profitability. Greater the ROI, better the profitability.

q2.q: State any two limitations of ratio analysis.
q2.a: (i) Ratios are only means and not an end in themselves. (ii) Accuracy of ratios depends on the accuracy of financial information. (Also: need for consistency, non-availability of standards, ignore price level changes.)

q3.q: Explain the objectives of ratio analysis.
q3.a:
1. **To simplify accounting figures.**
2. **To facilitate analysis of financial statements.**
3. **To analyse the operational efficiency of a business.**
4. **To help in budgeting and forecasting.**
5. **To facilitate intra-firm and inter-firm comparison of performance.**

q3.q: What is inventory conversion period? How is it calculated?
q3.a:
- Inventory conversion period is the **time taken to sell the inventory**. A shorter period indicates more efficiency in inventory management.
- Inventory conversion period (in days) = Number of days in a year ÷ Inventory turnover ratio.
- Inventory conversion period (in months) = Number of months in a year ÷ Inventory turnover ratio.
- Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory.

q3.q: How is operating profit ascertained?
q3.a:
- **Operating profit = Revenue from operations – Operating cost.**
- Operating cost = Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses.
- Operating expenses = Employee benefit expenses + Depreciation + Office and administration, selling and distribution expenses.
- Non-operating items (interest, loss on sale of fixed assets, non-operating income) are excluded.
- Alternatively, Operating profit = Gross profit – Operating expenses.

q3.q: State any three advantages of ratio analysis.
q3.a:
1. **Measuring operational efficiency:** relationship between operating cost and revenues and comparison with past ratios.
2. **Measuring financial solvency:** ascertains liquidity (short-term) and long-term solvency.
3. **Facilitating investment decisions:** helps management decide profitable avenues of investment.
(Also: analysing profitability, intra-firm and inter-firm comparison.)

q3.q: Bring out the limitations of ratio analysis.
q3.a:
1. **Ratios are only means:** not an end; analysis must be done by management or experts with the help of ratios.
2. **Accuracy of financial information:** inaccurate statements give inaccurate ratios.
3. **Consistency in preparation of financial statements:** inter-firm comparison is meaningful only if uniform accounting procedures are followed.
4. **Non-availability of standards or norms:** only a few ratios have universally recognised standards.
5. **Change in price level:** ratios are based on historical data and do not reflect current values.

acc.title: Computerised Accounting System – Tally
acc.intro: Accounts are now kept on computers. This unit explains computerised accounting (CAS), its applications, accounting reports, information systems, and how to use Tally.ERP 9 – creating a company, groups, ledgers and the six voucher types. MCQs and short answers on voucher types and shortcut keys are very common.

pts: System of maintaining accounts using computers; transactions are **inputs**, processed through accounting **software** to generate **reports**.
**Maintaining accounting records** – easy, long period, little physical space, fast retrieval.
**Inventory management** – identifies fast/slow-moving and obsolete stock; instant stock levels.
**Pay roll preparation** – attendance, salary, deductions (PF, income tax).
**Report generation** – routine and special purpose reports.
**Data import/export** – within and outside the organisation.
**Taxation** – computing, deducting and depositing taxes.
Maintaining up-to-date records with accounting software; entry made in **one field** and the software automatically relates it to all other relevant records.

Compilation of accounting information from records. **Routine reports:** day book/journal, ledger, trial balance, income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement. **Special purpose reports:** prepared as per user requirement.
Steps in designing: define objective → specify structure → create database queries.
**MIS** – information for decision making at all levels; includes manufacturing, marketing, HR and accounting information systems.
**AIS** – collects financial data, processes them and provides information; exchanges data with other systems (e.g. wages need manufacturing and HR data).
Widely used accounting and inventory software; **Tally.ERP 9** introduced in **2009**; updated for **GST** in **2017**; follows double entry.
Education mode – only dates **1, 2 and 31** can be used.
Create company: Company Info > Create Company. **Gateway of Tally** = main screen with Masters, Transactions and Reports.
Close Tally: Esc > Yes or **Ctrl + Q**. Select company: **F1**. Company features: **F11** (Accounting features – "Maintain accounts only: Yes").

**Group** = collection of ledgers of the same nature; 28+ predefined groups (Primary – Capital Account, Current Liabilities, Fixed Assets, Current Assets…; Sub-groups – Reserves & Surplus, Sundry Creditors, Sundry Debtors…).
**Predefined ledgers:** **Cash** and **Profit & Loss A/c**. Predefined group/ledger cannot be deleted (only name altered); user-defined can be deleted with **Alt + D**.
Ledger creation: Gateway of Tally > Masters > Accounts Info > Ledgers > Single Ledger > Create.
**F4 Contra** – cash ↔ bank (deposit/withdrawal).
**F5 Payment** – cash/bank paid (cash/bank credited).
**F6 Receipt** – cash/bank received (cash/bank debited).
**F7 Journal** – non-cash items: depreciation, provisions, credit purchase of assets, rectification.
**F8 Sales** – cash and credit sales of goods.
**F9 Purchase** – cash and credit purchases of goods.
Trial balance: Gateway of Tally > Reports > Display > Trial Balance (Alt+F1 detailed).
P&L A/c / Balance sheet / Ratio analysis / Day book: Gateway of Tally > Reports > … or **F10: A/c Reports**.

q2.a: Automated accounting is an approach to maintain up-to-date accounting records with the aid of accounting software. Software packages allow entry in one field or place, and from there the software automatically relates the transaction to all other relevant records.
Accounting report is a compilation of accounting information derived from the accounting records of a business concern. They are classified as routine reports and special purpose reports.
(a) Day books / Journal (b) Ledger (c) Trial balance (d) Income statement (e) Balance sheet (also cash flow statement).

Accounting Information System collects financial data, processes them and provides information to the various users. It requires data from other information systems (manufacturing, marketing, human resources) and also provides data to them.

q2.q: What is a group in Tally.ERP 9?
q2.a: In Tally, a group is a collection of ledgers of the same nature. There are predefined groups (e.g. Capital Account, Current Assets, Fixed Assets, Sundry Debtors) classified into assets, liabilities, income and expenses; additional groups can also be created.

q3.q: Write a brief note on accounting vouchers.
q3.a:
A voucher is a document containing details of a transaction; transactions are recorded through voucher entries. Major vouchers in Tally:
- **Receipt voucher (F6):** all receipts in cash or bank; cash/bank debited.
- **Payment voucher (F5):** all payments in cash or bank; cash/bank credited.
- **Contra voucher (F4):** transactions involving both cash and bank – deposit or withdrawal.
- **Purchase voucher (F9):** cash and credit purchases of goods.
- **Sales voucher (F8):** cash and credit sales of goods.
- **Journal voucher (F7):** transactions other than cash, bank, purchases and sales – e.g. depreciation, provision for bad debts.
Voucher creation contains name and number, date, particulars, debit/credit and narration.

q3.q: What are the pre-defined ledgers available in Tally.ERP 9?
q3.a:
- Tally has **two predefined ledgers – Cash and Profit & Loss A/c**.
- The user creates other ledgers as required (Gateway of Tally > Masters > Accounts Info > Ledgers > Single Ledger > Create), giving the name and the group.
- Predefined ledgers cannot be deleted; only their names can be altered.

q3.q: Mention the commonly used voucher types in Tally.ERP 9.
q3.a: (i) Receipt voucher – F6 (ii) Payment voucher – F5 (iii) Contra voucher – F4 (iv) Purchase voucher – F9 (v) Sales voucher – F8 (vi) Journal voucher – F7. The list can be viewed through Gateway of Tally > Masters > Accounts Info > Voucher Types > Display.

q3.q: Explain how to view profit and loss statement in Tally.ERP 9.
q3.a:
- **F10: A/c Reports > Profit & Loss A/c > Alt F1 (detailed)**, or
- **Gateway of Tally > Reports > Profit & Loss A/c > Alt F1 (detailed)**.
- Alt+F1 gives the detailed view showing individual ledgers under each group.

q3.q: Explain any five applications of computerised accounting system.
q3.a:
1. **Maintaining accounting records:** easily and efficiently for long periods; little physical space; fast, accurate retrieval.
2. **Inventory management:** identifies fast-moving, slow-moving and obsolete stock; instant information on inventory levels.
3. **Pay roll preparation:** records attendance, computes salary and deductions like PF and income tax.
4. **Report generation:** routine and special purpose reports.
5. **Data import/export:** data can be imported from or exported to users within and outside the organisation.
6. **Taxation:** computes, deducts and deposits taxes to Government.

bm.title: Applications of Matrices and Determinants
bm.intro: This chapter uses matrices to solve real problems: finding the rank of a matrix, testing whether a system of equations is consistent (rank method), solving equations by Cramer's rule, and predicting market shares using transition probability matrices. Every year it gives sure-shot 1, 2, 3 and 5 mark questions.

pts: The **rank** of A, written ρ(A), is the **order of the largest non-zero minor** of A.
ρ(A) ≥ 0; for an m × n matrix, ρ(A) ≤ minimum of {m, n}.
Rank of a **zero (null) matrix is 0**; rank of a **non-singular** n × n matrix (|A| ≠ 0) is **n**; rank of the unit matrix Iₙ is n.

**Elementary transformations:** (i) interchange two rows Rᵢ ↔ Rⱼ (ii) multiply a row by a non-zero number Rᵢ → kRᵢ (iii) add a multiple of another row Rᵢ → Rᵢ + kRⱼ. (Same for columns.) Row and column operations are never mixed in one step.
**Equivalent matrices:** A ~ B if one is obtained from the other by elementary transformations; equivalent matrices have the same rank.
**Echelon form:** every zero row lies below the non-zero rows and the number of zeros before the first non-zero entry increases row by row. **Rank = number of non-zero rows** in echelon form.
2 × 2 or 3 × 3: if |A| ≠ 0, rank = order. If |A| = 0, look for a non-zero minor of the next lower order.
Larger / rectangular: reduce to echelon form using row operations, count non-zero rows.
Write AX = B and the **augmented matrix [A, B]**; reduce to echelon form.
**ρ(A) = ρ([A,B]) = n** (number of unknowns) → consistent, **unique solution**.
**ρ(A) = ρ([A,B]) < n** → consistent, **infinitely many solutions** (put z = k).
**ρ(A) ≠ ρ([A,B])** → **inconsistent**, no solution.
Gabriel Cramer (Swiss, born 1704, Geneva) published the rule in **1750**.
Applicable only when **Δ ≠ 0** (determinant of the coefficient matrix).
Two variables: x = Δx/Δ, y = Δy/Δ.
Three variables: x = Δx/Δ, y = Δy/Δ, z = Δz/Δ, where Δx is Δ with the x-column replaced by the constants.
If |A| = 0 the system has either no solution or infinitely many solutions.
|adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹.
One-stage transition probability Pⱼₖ: probability of moving from state j to state k in one step; **Pⱼₖ ≥ 0** and **each row sums to 1**.
**Next state** = (present shares) × T.
**Equilibrium:** (A B) T = (A B) with A + B = 1. Solve one equation with B = 1 – A.

q2.q: When is a system of equations said to be consistent?
q2.a: A system of equations is said to be consistent if it has at least one set of solution; otherwise it is inconsistent. It is consistent when ρ([A,B]) = ρ(A).

q2.q: What is a transition probability matrix?
q2.a: The transition probabilities Pⱼₖ (probability of moving from state j to state k in one step) written in matrix form P = [Pⱼₖ] is called a transition probability matrix. Pⱼₖ ≥ 0 and the sum of each row is 1.

bm.title: Integral Calculus – I
bm.intro: Integration is the reverse of differentiation. This chapter covers standard indefinite integrals (Types I–VII), integration by parts, substitution, special integrals using completing the square, definite integrals and their properties, the Gamma integral and definite integral as the limit of a sum. It carries the largest share of marks in Business Maths – practise the standard forms daily.

pts: If d/dx[F(x)] = f(x), then F(x) is a **primitive (anti-derivative)** of f(x) and ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + c, where c is the **constant of integration**.

∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ –1); ∫(ax+b)ⁿ dx = (ax+b)ⁿ⁺¹/[a(n+1)] + c.

bm.title: Integral Calculus – II
bm.intro: This chapter applies integration: finding the area bounded by curves, and in economics and commerce – total cost from marginal cost, revenue and demand from marginal revenue, profit, elasticity, inventory cost, annuity, and consumer's and producer's surplus. Problems are formula-driven and score well.

pts: The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is geometrically the **area** bounded by y = f(x), the x-axis and the ordinates x = a, x = b.
Area above x-axis: A = ∫ₐᵇ y dx. Area **below** x-axis: A = –∫ₐᵇ y dx (take the absolute value).
Area with y-axis between y = c and y = d (right of y-axis): A = ∫꜀ᵈ x dy; left of y-axis: –∫꜀ᵈ x dy.
**Area between two curves** f(x) ≥ g(x): A = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) – g(x)]dx.
Use symmetry: parabola y² = 4ax is symmetric about x-axis → area = 2 × area in first quadrant; circle x² + y² = a² → 4 × first quadrant (area πa²).
Latus rectum of y² = 4ax is x = a.
**Cost function:** C = ∫MC dx + k; k = fixed cost (C when x = 0). Average cost AC = C/x.
**Revenue function:** R = ∫MR dx + k; k found using R = 0 when x = 0. **Demand (price) function:** P = R/x; Average revenue AR = R/x.
**Profit:** P = ∫(MR – MC)dx + k; k = – fixed cost when x = 0.
**Elasticity of demand:** η_d = –(p/x)(dx/dp). Given elasticity, separate variables and integrate to get the demand function.
**Total sale/growth over time:** ∫₀ʳ f(t)dt.
**Inventory carrying cost:** C₁∫₀ᵀ I(x)dx, C₁ = holding cost per unit per day.
**Amount of annuity** (continuous compounding): A = ∫₀ᴺ p e^(rt) dt.
Gain to consumers who were willing to pay more than the market price p₀.
**CS = ∫₀^x₀ f(x)dx – x₀p₀** (area under demand curve minus rectangle).
Gain to producers who were willing to supply below the market price.
**PS = x₀p₀ – ∫₀^x₀ g(x)dx** (rectangle minus area under supply curve).
**Equilibrium:** demand = supply (p_d = p_s) gives x₀ and p₀.

terms: Rate of change of total cost with respect to output, dC/dx.
Rate of change of total revenue with respect to output, dR/dx.
Cost when output is zero; the constant of integration in the cost function.
Gain to consumers willing to pay more than the market price.
Gain to producers willing to sell below the market price.

bm.title: Differential Equations
bm.intro: A differential equation connects a function with its derivatives. You will learn order and degree, forming differential equations by eliminating constants, and solving first order equations (variables separable, homogeneous, linear) and second order linear equations with constant coefficients – along with business applications like growth, cost and market equilibrium.

pts: **Differential equation:** an equation involving an independent variable, a dependent variable and derivatives of the dependent variable.
**Order:** order of the highest derivative present. **Degree:** power of the highest order derivative after making the equation free of radicals and fractions in derivatives.
**Formation:** differentiate the given family as many times as the number of arbitrary constants and eliminate them. Number of constants = order of the equation.
**General solution** contains as many arbitrary constants as the order; **particular solution** is obtained by giving values to the constants.
Form f(x)dx = g(y)dy → integrate both sides: ∫f(x)dx = ∫g(y)dy + c.
dy/dx = f(x, y)/g(x, y) where f, g are homogeneous of the **same degree**, i.e. dy/dx = F(y/x).
Put **y = vx**, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx → separate: dv/(F(v) – v) = dx/x → integrate → replace v = y/x.
If dx/dy = F(x/y), put x = vy.
**dy/dx + Py = Q** (P, Q functions of x). **I.F. = e^(∫P dx)**. Solution: **y (I.F.) = ∫Q (I.F.)dx + c**.
dx/dy + Px = Q (P, Q functions of y): I.F. = e^(∫P dy); x (I.F.) = ∫Q (I.F.)dy + c.
Useful: e^(log f(x)) = f(x); e^(–log x) = 1/x.

q2.q: Define order and degree of a differential equation.
q2.a: The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest order derivative occurring in it. The degree is the power (exponent) of the highest order derivative after the equation is made free from radicals and fractions as far as derivatives are concerned.

q2.q: What is a homogeneous differential equation?
q2.a: A differential equation of the form dy/dx = f(x, y)/g(x, y) is homogeneous if f(x, y) and g(x, y) are homogeneous functions of the same degree in x and y; it can be written as dy/dx = F(y/x). It is solved by putting y = vx.

bm.title: Numerical Methods
bm.intro: Numerical methods help estimate unknown values from a table. You will learn finite differences (Δ, ∇, E operators), finding missing terms, and interpolation – graphic method, Newton's forward and backward formulas and Lagrange's formula. Problems are mechanical: build the difference table carefully and substitute.

pts: For equally spaced x with interval h: **Forward difference** Δf(x) = f(x + h) – f(x); Δy₀ = y₁ – y₀, Δ²y₀ = Δy₁ – Δy₀, …
**Backward difference** ∇f(x) = f(x) – f(x – h); ∇yₙ = yₙ – yₙ₋₁.
**Shift operator** Ef(x) = f(x + h); Eⁿf(x) = f(x + nh); E⁻¹f(x) = f(x – h).
Properties: Δc = 0 for a constant; Δ[cf(x)] = cΔf(x); Δ[f ± g] = Δf ± Δg; ΔᵐΔⁿf = Δᵐ⁺ⁿf.
For a polynomial of degree n, the **nth differences are constant** and (n+1)th differences are zero.
If n values are known, assume a polynomial of degree n – 1, so Δⁿy = 0, i.e. (E – 1)ⁿ y₀ = 0. Expand using binomial coefficients (1, 4, 6, 4, 1 for n = 4; 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1 for n = 5).
Two missing values → write two equations (k = 0 and k = 1) and solve.
Estimating y for an x **within** the given range = **interpolation**; outside the range = **extrapolation**. x is the **argument**, y the **entry**.
**Graphic method:** plot points, draw a free-hand smooth curve and read the value (drawback: only approximate).
**Newton's forward formula** – equal intervals, value near the **beginning** of the table; n = (x – x₀)/h.
**Newton's backward formula** – equal intervals, value near the **end**; n = (x – xₙ)/h (negative).
**Lagrange's formula** – for **equal or unequal** intervals.
For class intervals (marks/weights), convert to **cumulative ('less than') frequencies** before interpolating.

bm.title: Random Variable and Mathematical Expectation
bm.intro: A random variable attaches numbers to the outcomes of a random experiment. This chapter covers discrete and continuous random variables, probability mass and density functions, distribution functions, and the mathematical expectation (mean) and variance with their properties. It gives both theory (2/3 marks) and numerical (3/5 marks) questions.

pts: A **random variable (r.v.)** is a real valued function defined on a sample space S, taking values in (–∞, ∞); its possible values are numerical outcomes of a random experiment.
Examples: number of heads when a coin is tossed 8 times; return on an investment in one year; faces on rolling a die; customers arriving at a bank per hour; sale volume of a store.
If X₁, X₂ are r.v.s and C a constant, CX₁, X₁ + X₂, X₁X₂, X₁ – X₂ are also r.v.s.
Two types: **discrete** and **continuous**.
Assumes a **finite** number of values or an infinite sequence of **countable** real numbers (marks in a test, number of red marbles, telephone calls, cars sold).
**Probability mass function (p.m.f.)** p(x) = P(X = xᵢ): conditions (i) p(xᵢ) ≥ 0 for all i (ii) Σp(xᵢ) = 1.
**Cumulative distribution function:** F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = Σ p(xᵢ) for xᵢ ≤ x – a **step function** for a discrete r.v.
Can take **any value (integral or fractional)** in an interval (amount of water in a bottle, speed of a car, electricity consumption, height, weight, travel time).
**Probability density function (p.d.f.)** f(x): P(t₁ ≤ X ≤ t₂) = ∫ f(x)dx from t₁ to t₂; conditions f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫₋∞^∞ f(x)dx = 1. P(X = c) = 0 for a continuous r.v.
**Distribution function:** F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫₋∞ˣ f(t)dt.
F is monotone non-decreasing: F(a) ≤ F(b) for a < b; continuous from the right.

**Expected value** = weighted average of the values of a r.v., weights being the probabilities. Discrete: E(X) = Σx p(x); continuous: E(X) = ∫x f(x)dx. It is the "centre of gravity" of the distribution.
**Variance** = weighted average of squared deviations from the mean: **Var(X) = E[X – E(X)]² = E(X²) – [E(X)]²**. S.D. = √Var(X).
E(a) = a; E(aX) = aE(X); E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; if X ≥ 0 then E(X) ≥ 0.
E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y); E(X – Y) = E(X) – E(Y).
rth raw moment μ′ᵣ = E(Xʳ); rth central moment μᵣ = E[(X – μ)ʳ]. μ′₁ = mean, μ₁ = 0, μ₂ = variance.

q2.a: A random variable (r.v.) is a real valued function defined on a sample space S and taking values in (–∞, ∞), or whose possible values are numerical outcomes of a random experiment.

A variable which can assume finite number of possible values or an infinite sequence of countable real numbers is called a discrete random variable. Examples: marks obtained in a test, number of telephone calls at a particular time.

q2.q: What do you understand by continuous random variable?
q2.a: A random variable X which can take on any value (integral as well as fraction) in the interval is called a continuous random variable. Examples: speed of a car, height of people, weight of students.

q2.q: What do you understand by Mathematical expectation?
q2.a: The average value of a random phenomenon is termed its mathematical expectation or expected value. It is a weighted average of the values a random variable may assume, the weights being the probabilities.

q2.q: How do you define variance in terms of Mathematical expectation?
q2.a: Expected value of [X – E(X)]² is called the variance of the random variable: Var(X) = E[X – E(X)]² = E(X²) – [E(X)]².

q2.q: Define Mathematical expectation in terms of discrete random variable.
q2.a: Let X be a discrete random variable with probability mass function p(x). Then its expected value is E(X) = Σ x p(x).

q2.q: State the definition of Mathematical expectation using continuous random variable.
q2.a: If X is a continuous random variable and f(x) is the value of its probability density function at x, the expected value of X is E(X) = ∫₋∞^∞ x f(x) dx.

q3.q: Explain what are the types of random variable?
q3.a:
Random variables are of two types:
- **Discrete random variable:** assumes a finite number of values or an infinite sequence of countable real numbers, e.g. marks obtained in a test, number of red marbles in a jar, number of cars sold in a month. Described by a probability mass function.
- **Continuous random variable:** can take any value (integral as well as fraction) in an interval, e.g. amount of water in a bottle, speed of a car, electricity consumption, height of people. Described by a probability density function.

q3.q: Distinguish between discrete and continuous random variable.
q3.a:
| Discrete random variable | Continuous random variable |
| Takes finite or countably infinite values | Takes any value in an interval |
| Described by probability mass function p(x) | Described by probability density function f(x) |
| Σ p(x) = 1 | ∫ f(x)dx = 1 |
| P(X = x) can be positive | P(X = c) = 0 |
| E(X) = Σ x p(x) | E(X) = ∫ x f(x)dx |
| Distribution function is a step function | Distribution function is continuous |
| e.g. number of heads, marks | e.g. height, weight, time |

q3.q: Explain the distribution function of a random variable.
q3.a:
- Discrete: F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = Σ p(xᵢ) for xᵢ ≤ x (cumulative distribution function).
- Continuous: F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫₋∞ˣ f(t)dt, –∞ < x < ∞.
- It gives the probability that X takes a value less than or equal to x; f(x) = F′(x).

q3.q: Explain the terms (i) probability mass function, (ii) probability density function and (iii) probability distribution function.
q3.a:
- **(i) p.m.f.:** for a discrete r.v. X with values x₁, x₂, …, p(x) = P(X = xᵢ); p(xᵢ) ≥ 0 and Σp(xᵢ) = 1.
- **(ii) p.d.f.:** for a continuous r.v., f(x) such that P(t₁ ≤ X ≤ t₂) = ∫ f(x)dx over [t₁, t₂]; f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫₋∞^∞ f(x)dx = 1.
- **(iii) Distribution function:** F(x) = P(X ≤ x) – sum of p(x) (discrete) or integral of f(x) (continuous) up to x.

q3.q: What are the properties of (i) discrete random variable and (ii) continuous random variable?
q3.a:
- **(i) Discrete:** p(xᵢ) ≥ 0 for all i; Σ p(xᵢ) = 1; P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) – F(a).
- **(ii) Continuous:** f(x) ≥ 0; ∫₋∞^∞ f(x)dx = 1; P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx; P(X = c) = 0.

q3.q: State the properties of distribution function.
q3.a:
1. 0 ≤ F(x) ≤ 1, –∞ < x < ∞.
2. F(–∞) = 0 and F(+∞) = 1.
3. F is monotone non-decreasing: F(a) ≤ F(b) for a < b.
4. F is continuous from the right.
5. F′(x) = f(x) ≥ 0.
6. P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = F(b) – F(a).

q3.q: What are the properties of Mathematical expectation?
q3.a:
1. E(a) = a, where 'a' is a constant.
2. E(aX) = aE(X).
3. E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, where a and b are constants.
4. If X ≥ 0, then E(X) ≥ 0.
5. V(a) = 0.
6. V(aX + b) = a²V(X).

bm.title: Probability Distributions
bm.intro: Three theoretical distributions dominate business statistics: Binomial (fixed number of yes/no trials), Poisson (rare events) and Normal (continuous, bell-shaped). Learn their definitions, conditions, mean and variance, properties and how to read the normal table – this chapter offers easy 2-mark theory and reliable 5-mark problems.

pts: **Discrete distributions:** Binomial, Poisson. **Continuous distribution:** Normal.
Discovered by **James Bernoulli** (1700), published posthumously in **1713**.
**Bernoulli trial:** a random experiment with only two outcomes, success S and failure F, with probabilities p and q (e.g. tossing a coin, getting even/odd on a die).
**Definition:** X follows binomial distribution with parameters n and p if P(X = x) = nCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ, x = 0, 1, …, n; q = 1 – p. Written X ~ B(n, p).
**Conditions:** (1) number of trials n is finite (2) trials are independent (3) probability of success p is constant for each trial (4) each trial has only two outcomes – success or failure.
**Mean = np, Variance = npq**, S.D. = √(npq).
**Properties:** symmetrical if p = q = 0.5; positively skewed if p < 0.5, negatively skewed if p > 0.5; **variance is less than mean** (npq < np).
If p + q > 1 or q > 1 from given mean and S.D., the statement is impossible.
Derived in **1837** by French mathematician **Simeon D. Poisson**; approximates binomial when n is large and p is close to zero (rare events).
Examples: bacteria per cubic centimetre; printing mistakes per page; alpha particles emitted in a fraction of a second; road accidents per day; lightnings per second.
**Limiting case of binomial when:** (i) n → ∞ (ii) p → 0 (iii) np = λ is finite.
**Mean = Variance = λ** – the only distribution in which mean and variance are equal.
Introduced by **De Moivre (1733)**; developed by Laplace and Gauss.
**Limiting case of binomial when:** n → ∞ and neither p nor q is very small.

**Properties of the normal curve:** (i) bell-shaped and symmetrical about x = μ (ii) mean = median = mode (iii) x-axis is an asymptote (tails never touch) (iv) no portion lies below x-axis (v) points of inflexion at x = μ ± σ (vi) unimodal (vii) maximum ordinate 1/(σ√(2π)) at x = μ (viii) total area = 1: μ ± σ → 68.27%, μ ± 2σ → 95.45%, μ ± 3σ → 99.73%.
Use the table of P(0 < Z < z). Symmetry: P(Z < –a) = P(Z > a) = 0.5 – P(0 < Z < a).

A random variable X is said to follow a normal distribution with parameters mean μ and variance σ² if its probability density function is f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] exp{–½((x – μ)/σ)²}, –∞ < x < ∞, –∞ < μ < ∞, σ > 0.

A random variable Z = (X – μ)/σ follows the standard normal distribution. Z is called the standard normal variate with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, i.e. Z ~ N(0, 1), with p.d.f. f(z) = (1/√(2π)) e^(–z²/2).

q3.q: Write down the conditions for which the binomial distribution can be used.
q3.a:
1. The number of trials 'n' is finite.
2. The trials are independent of each other.
3. The probability of success 'p' is constant for each trial.
4. In every trial there are only two possible outcomes – success or failure.

q3.q: Mention the properties of binomial distribution.
q3.a:
1. Binomial distribution is symmetrical if p = q = 0.5. It is skew symmetric if p ≠ q; positively skewed if p < 0.5 and negatively skewed if p > 0.5.
2. For binomial distribution, variance is less than mean: npq = (np)q < np.
3. Mean = np, variance = npq; parameters are n and p.

q3.q: Write the conditions for which the poisson distribution is a limiting case of binomial distribution.
q3.a:
(i) n, the number of trials, is indefinitely large, i.e. n → ∞.
(ii) p, the constant probability of success in each trial, is very small, i.e. p → 0.
(iii) np = λ is finite, so p = λ/n and q = 1 – λ/n, where λ is a positive real number.

q3.q: Mention the properties of poisson distribution.
q3.a:
1. Poisson distribution is the only distribution in which the mean and variance are equal (both = λ).
2. It is a discrete distribution with a single parameter λ.
3. It is the limiting form of binomial distribution when n is large, p is small and np is finite.

q3.q: Write down the conditions in which the Normal distribution is a limiting case of binomial distribution.
q3.a:
(i) n, the number of trials, is infinitely large, i.e. n → ∞.
(ii) Neither p (nor q) is very small.

q5.q: Write down any five chief characteristics of Normal probability curve.
q5.a:
1. The curve is bell-shaped and symmetrical about the line x = μ.
2. Mean, median and mode of the distribution coincide.
3. The x-axis is an asymptote to the curve (tails never touch the horizontal axis).
4. No portion of the curve lies below the x-axis, as f(x) can never be negative.
5. The points of inflexion of the curve are x = μ ± σ.
6. The curve has a single peak, i.e. it is unimodal.
7. As x increases numerically, f(x) decreases rapidly; the maximum probability occurs at x = μ and is 1/(σ√(2π)).
8. The total area under the curve is unity: about 68.27% lies between μ ± σ, 95.45% between μ ± 2σ and 99.73% between μ ± 3σ.

q5.q: Derive the mean and variance of binomial distribution.
q5.a:
**Mean:** E(X) = Σ x · nCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ = np Σ (n–1)C(x–1) pˣ⁻¹ qⁿ⁻ˣ = np(q + p)ⁿ⁻¹ = **np** (since p + q = 1).
**E(X²)** = Σ [x(x – 1) + x] nCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ = n(n – 1)p² (q + p)ⁿ⁻² + np = n(n – 1)p² + np.
**Variance** = E(X²) – [E(X)]² = n²p² – np² + np – n²p² = np(1 – p) = **npq**.

q5.q: Derive the mean and variance of poisson distribution.
q5.a:
**Mean:** E(X) = Σ x e^(–λ)λˣ/x! = λe^(–λ) Σ λˣ⁻¹/(x – 1)! = λe^(–λ)(1 + λ + λ²/2! + …) = λe^(–λ)e^λ = **λ**.
**E(X²)** = Σ [x(x – 1) + x] e^(–λ)λˣ/x! = λ²e^(–λ)Σ λˣ⁻²/(x – 2)! + λ = λ² + λ.
**Variance** = λ² + λ – λ² = **λ**.

bm.title: Sampling Techniques and Statistical Inference
bm.intro: Instead of studying every member of a population, we study a sample and draw conclusions. This chapter covers population, sample, parameter and statistic, random sampling methods (simple random, stratified, systematic), sampling and non-sampling errors, standard error, estimation (point, interval, confidence limits) and testing of hypothesis using the Z-test for a single mean. Theory-heavy – learn definitions in book language.

pts: **Sampling** is the process of selecting a representative sample from a population (housewife tasting food, blood test, grain merchant).

**Population** – the group of individuals under study (people, products, items). **Finite** (countable, e.g. weights of class XII students) or **infinite** (uncountable, e.g. grains in a sack, germs in a body).
**Sample** – a group selected so that it represents the population; **sample size** – number of individuals in the sample.
**Parameter** – statistical constant of the population (μ, σ²). **Statistic** – any measure computed from the sample.
Pioneer: **P. V. Sukhatme** – random sampling in agricultural statistics.
Non-random (non-probability) and **Random (probability)** sampling.

Random sample: each item has an equal chance of selection. "Every member of a parent population has had equal chances of being included" – **Dr. Yates**; "A random sample is a sample selected in such a way that every item in the population has an equal chance of being included" – **Harper**.
Every unit has an **equal and independent chance**; usually **without replacement**; probability of a unit at the first draw = 1/N.
**Lottery method** (finite population; slips of same size, shape, colour; unrestricted random sampling).
**Random number tables:** L.H.C. Tippett (most used), Fisher and Yates, Kendall and Smith, Rand Corporation.
Merits: no personal bias; economical; needs little prior knowledge. Demerits: needs complete up-to-date list; small samples may not represent.

Population (heterogeneous) divided into homogeneous, non-overlapping **strata**; a random sample is drawn from each stratum; together they form the stratified sample (e.g. legislative areas, districts).
Merits: more representative; small sample with accuracy; easy to administer; reduces time and expense. Demerits: costly to stratify; bias if improper; faulty classification increases variability.
Sampling interval **k = N/n**; choose the first unit at random from the first k units, then every kth unit.
Merits: simple and convenient; distributes sample evenly; saves time. Demerits: not truly random; difficult if N is not a multiple of n.
**Sampling errors** – arise by chance in the course of sampling: faulty selection, substitution of a convenient sample, faulty demarcation of sampling units.
**Non-sampling errors** – human factors: negligence of investigator/respondent, untrained investigators, wrong questionnaire, wrong statistical measure, incomplete investigation.
**Sampling distribution** – frequency distribution of a statistic computed from all samples of the same size from the same population (NCn samples).
**Standard error (S.E.)** – standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic.
Statistical inference has two branches: **estimation** and **testing of hypothesis**.
**Estimation** – obtaining the most likely value of a parameter using a statistic. **Estimator** – the sample statistic used. **Estimate** – a specific observed value of the estimator.
Good estimator: **unbiasedness** (E(T) = θ), **consistency**, **efficiency** (E = V₁/V₂ ≤ 1), **sufficiency**.
**Point estimation** – a single value; **interval estimation** – limits within which the parameter is expected to lie.
**Confidence interval** (c₁, c₂) with P(c₁ < θ < c₂) = 1 – α; (1 – α) = confidence coefficient. For mean: x̄ ± Z_(α/2) σ/√n.
Initiated by **J. Neyman and E. S. Pearson**; also called statistical decision making.
**Null hypothesis H₀** (R. A. Fisher): "the hypothesis which is tested for possible rejection under the assumption that it is true", e.g. H₀: μ = μ₀.
**Alternative hypothesis H₁** – complementary to H₀: μ ≠ μ₀ (two-tailed), μ > μ₀ (right-tailed), μ < μ₀ (left-tailed).
**Type I error** – rejecting H₀ when it is true; **Type II error** – accepting H₀ when it is false.

**Critical region** – region leading to rejection of H₀; **level of significance α** – probability of type I error (5% or 1%), fixed in advance; **critical value** – value of test statistic separating critical and acceptance regions.
Large sample: n > 30. Test statistic **Z = (x̄ – μ)/(σ/√n)**. If |Z| < Z_α → accept H₀ (not significant); if |Z| > Z_α → reject H₀.
Steps: (1) H₀ (2) H₁ (3) level of significance (4) test statistic (5) conclusion.

mcq.q: The standard error of sample mean is

q2.a: The group of individuals considered under study is called population. It refers not only to people but to all items chosen for the study, e.g. number of bikes manufactured in a day, number of students. It may be finite or infinite.
A selection of a group of individuals from a population in such a way that it represents the population is called a sample. The number of individuals included in a sample is called the sample size.
Any statistical measure computed from a sample is known as a statistic, e.g. sample mean x̄, sample variance s².
The statistical constants of the population like mean (μ) and variance (σ²) are referred to as population parameters.

q2.q: What is sampling distribution of a statistic?
q2.a: Sampling distribution of a statistic is the frequency distribution which is formed with various values of a statistic computed from different samples of the same size drawn from the same population.
The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic is known as its standard error (S.E.). E.g. S.E. of sample mean = σ/√n.

q2.q: State any two merits of simple random sampling.
q2.a: (1) Personal bias is completely eliminated. (2) This method is economical as it saves time, money and labour. (Also: requires minimum knowledge about the population in advance.)

q2.q: State any two demerits of systematic random sampling.
q2.a: (1) Systematic samples are not random samples. (2) If N is not a multiple of n, the sampling interval k cannot be an integer, so sample selection becomes difficult.

q2.q: State any two merits for systematic random sampling.
q2.a: (1) This is a simple and convenient method. (2) It distributes the sample more evenly over the entire listed population. (Also: time and work are much reduced.)

q2.q: Mention two branches of statistical inference?
q2.a: (i) Estimation (ii) Testing of hypothesis.
Any sample statistic which is used to estimate an unknown population parameter is called an estimator.
When we observe a specific numerical value of our estimator, we call that value an estimate; i.e., an estimate is a specific observed value of a statistic.

When a single value is used as an estimate, the estimate is called a point estimate of the population parameter. E.g. 55, the mean mark of a sample of 5 students, taken as the mean mark of the whole class.
Finding limits within which the population parameter would be expected to lie is called interval estimation, e.g. "we are about 95% certain that θ lies between T – 2s and T + 2s".

For a small α (1% or 5%), constants c₁ and c₂ such that P(c₁ < θ < c₂ | t) = 1 – α are confidence limits; the interval (c₁, c₂) within which the unknown parameter is expected to lie is the confidence interval and (1 – α) is the confidence coefficient.

q2.q: What is null hypothesis? Give an example.
q2.a: According to Prof. R. A. Fisher, "Null hypothesis is the hypothesis which is tested for possible rejection under the assumption that it is true", denoted by H₀. Example: H₀: μ = μ₀ (population mean has the specified value μ₀).
Any hypothesis which is complementary to the null hypothesis is called the alternative hypothesis, denoted by H₁, e.g. H₁: μ ≠ μ₀, μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀.

A region corresponding to a test statistic in the sample space which tends to rejection of H₀ is called the critical region or region of rejection. The complementary region is the region of acceptance.

The value of the test statistic which separates the critical (rejection) region and the acceptance region is called the critical value or significant value. It depends on the level of significance and whether the test is two-tailed or single-tailed.
The probability of type I error is known as level of significance, denoted by α. Usually 5% or 1% is used and it is fixed in advance before collecting the sample.
The error of rejecting H₀ when it is true is called type I error.

When the hypothesis about the population parameter is rejected only for the value of the sample statistic falling into one of the tails of the sampling distribution, it is a one-tailed test, e.g. H₁: μ > μ₀ (right-tailed) or H₁: μ < μ₀ (left-tailed).

q3.q: State any three merits of stratified random sampling.
q3.a:
1. It is superior to a simple random sample because it ensures representation of all groups and is more representative of the population.
2. A stratified random sample can be kept small in size without losing its accuracy.
3. It is easy to administer if the population is sub-divided.
4. It reduces time and expenses when strata are geographical divisions already made by the government.

q3.q: Explain in detail about sampling error.
q3.a:
Errors which arise in the normal course of investigation or enumeration on account of chance are called sampling errors. They are inherent in the method of sampling and may arise accidentally without any bias. They arise due to:
- (a) Faulty selection of the sample by defective sampling technique.
- (b) The investigator substitutes a convenient sample if the original sample is not available.
- (c) Faulty demarcation of sampling units – in area surveys, including border lines depends on the investigator.

q3.q: Explain in detail about non-sampling error.
q3.a:
Errors that arise due to human factors, which vary from one investigator to another in selecting, estimating or using measuring instruments, are called non-sampling errors. They arise:
- (a) Due to negligence and carelessness on the part of investigator or respondents.
- (b) Due to lack of trained and qualified investigators.
- (c) Due to framing of a wrong questionnaire.
- (d) Due to applying a wrong statistical measure.
- (e) Due to incomplete investigation and sample survey.

q5.q: Explain in detail about simple random sampling with a suitable example.
q5.a:
In simple random sampling each and every unit in the population has an equal and independent chance of being selected. It is usually done without replacement; the probability of drawing any unit at the first draw is 1/N, at the second 1/(N – 1), and so on. Methods:
- **(A) Lottery method:** all items are numbered on slips of the same size, shape and colour, folded, shuffled and the required number drawn. E.g. to select 10 students out of 100, write all 100 roll numbers on slips and draw 10 blindfolded. Called unrestricted random sampling; not applicable to infinite populations.
- **(B) Random number table:** used when population is large. Tables: Tippett, Fisher and Yates, Kendall and Smith, Rand Corporation. Steps: number the units 1 to N; select a page of the table at random; select the required numbers from any row, column or diagonal (ignore numbers above N).
- **Merits:** personal bias eliminated; economical; requires minimum knowledge of the population. **Demerits:** needs a complete up-to-date list; small samples may not be representative.

q5.q: Explain the stratified random sampling with a suitable example.
q5.a:
When the population is heterogeneous, it is first divided into homogeneous sub-populations called **strata**, which do not overlap; then a sample of specified size is drawn at random from each stratum (lottery or random numbers); together they form the stratified random sample. Used for legislative areas in election polling, districts in a state.
**Example:** select 68 samples from a population of 500 with lower income 39%, middle income 38%, upper income 23%. Population in strata: 195, 190, 115. Samples = 68 × stratum/500 → 26.5 ≈ 26, 25.8 ≈ 26, 15.6 ≈ 16.
**Merits:** more representative; can be kept small; easy to administer; saves time and expense. **Demerits:** stratification needs money, time and expertise; improper stratification causes bias; faulty classification increases variability.

q5.q: Explain in detail about systematic random sampling with example.
q5.a:
In systematic sampling the first sample is selected at random from the first k units and then every kth member is included. Sampling interval **k = N/n**. It is used when a complete, up-to-date list is available (numerical, alphabetical or geographical order).
**Example:** to select 10 students from 100, k = 100/10 = 10. If the first random number from 1–10 is 5, the sample is 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85, 95. Similarly 20 items out of 6,000: k = 300; starting at 50 → 50, 350, 650, …, 5750.
**Merits:** simple and convenient; spreads sample evenly; saves time and work. **Demerits:** not truly random; difficult if N is not a multiple of n.

q5.q: Explain the procedures of testing of hypothesis.
q5.a:
1. **Null hypothesis:** set up H₀.
2. **Alternative hypothesis:** set up H₁ – this decides a two-tailed or single (right/left) tailed test.
3. **Level of significance:** choose α (5% or 1%) depending on reliability and permissible risk; fixed before drawing the sample.
4. **Test statistic:** compute Z = (t – E(t))/S.E.(t) ~ N(0, 1).
5. **Conclusion:** compare |Z| with the critical value Z_α. If |Z| < Z_α the difference is not significant and H₀ is accepted; if |Z| > Z_α it is significant and H₀ is rejected at level α.

q5.q: Explain in detail about the test of significance for single mean.
q5.a:
- If x₁, …, xₙ is a random sample of size n from a normal population with mean μ and variance σ², the sample mean x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n).
- For large samples (n > 30) the standard normal variate is Z = (x̄ – μ)/(σ/√n).
- Under H₀ that there is no significant difference between sample mean and population mean, the test statistic is Z = (x̄ – μ)/(σ/√n). If σ is unknown, use the sample s.
- Compare |Z| with the table value (1.96 at 5%, 2.58 at 1% for two-tailed) and accept or reject H₀.

tips: Write the five steps of hypothesis testing in every Z-test answer: H₀, H₁, α, Z, conclusion.
Use 1.96 (5%) and 2.58 (1%) for two-tailed; 1.645 / 2.33 for one-tailed.

examples.s:
H₀: μ = 9.5; H₁: μ ≠ 9.5 (two-tailed). Z = (10 – 9.5)/(3.5/√50) = 0.5/0.495 = 1.01.
|Z| = 1.01 < 1.96 → **H₀ accepted**; the claim is acceptable.

examples.q: (Example 8.15) Pens: claimed mean life 400 pages, σ = 20. Sample of 100 has mean 390. Test at 1%.
examples.s: Z = (390 – 400)/(20/10) = –5 → |Z| = 5 > 2.58 → **H₀ rejected**; the claim is rejected.

examples.q: (Example 8.17) Mean weekly sales 146.3 bars; after advertising, 400 stores give mean 153.7, SD 17.2. Was the campaign successful (5%)?
examples.s: H₀: μ = 146.3; H₁: μ > 146.3 (right-tailed). Z = 7.4/(17.2/20) = 7.4/0.86 = 8.605 > 1.645 → **H₀ rejected**; the campaign was successful.

bm.title: Applied Statistics
bm.intro: Applied statistics puts theory to work in business: Time Series (trend and seasonal variation), Index Numbers (Laspeyre's, Paasche's, Fisher's, cost of living, adequacy tests) and Statistical Quality Control (control charts for mean and range). Expect several theory questions plus a sure 5-mark problem on moving averages, least squares, Fisher's index or control limits.

pts: **Croxton & Cowden:** "A Time Series consists of data arranged chronologically." **Wessel & Wallet:** "When quantitative data are arranged in the order of their occurrence, the resulting series is called the Time Series."
Why/uses: analysis of past behaviour; forecasting and future plans; evaluation of current achievements; comparative studies between time periods.
**Secular trend** – general tendency to increase, decrease or stagnate over a **long period** (population, production, prices – upward; deaths, epidemics, mortality – downward).

**Seasonal variations** – periodic movements repeating **within one year**, due to nature, social customs and traditions (umbrellas in rainy season, cool drinks in summer, crackers at Deepawali, sugarcane in Pongal).
**Cyclic variations** – not uniformly periodic; a cycle usually **7 to 9 years**; business cycle: start – boom – depression – recovery.
**Irregular variations** – random, unpredictable, short-term (floods, wars, earthquakes, tsunami, strikes, lockouts).
**Additive model:** Y = T + S + C + I (components independent). **Multiplicative model:** Y = T × S × C × I (components may affect one another).
(i) **Freehand/graphic method** – plot, draw a smooth line through maximum points (simplest, most flexible).
(ii) **Semi-averages** – divide data into two halves (leave the middle year if odd), find average of each half, plot at mid-points and join.
(iii) **Moving averages** – 3-yearly: (a+b+c)/3, (b+c+d)/3 …; for even periods (4-yearly) average and then **centre** (average of two successive moving averages).

(iv) **Least squares** – best method; Σ(Y – Ŷ) = 0 and Σ(Y – Ŷ)² is least. Y = a + bX with normal equations ΣY = na + bΣX and ΣXY = aΣX + bΣX². Taking the middle year as origin (ΣX = 0): **a = ΣY/n, b = ΣXY/ΣX²**. For an even number of years X = (x – mean of middle years)/0.5.
Arrange data by months/quarters; find totals and averages for each season; find the **grand average**; **S.I. = Seasonal average ÷ Grand average × 100**.

**Wheldon:** "An Index Number is a device which shows by its variations the changes in a magnitude which is not capable of accurate measurements in itself or of direct valuation in practice." **Lawrence J. Kaplan:** "An Index number is a statistical measure of fluctuations in a variable arranged in the form of a series and using a base period for making comparisons."
Classification: **price index**, **quantity index**, **cost of living index**.
Uses: formulating decisions and management policies; studying trends and tendencies; determining inflation and deflation.
**Weighted index:** P₀₁ = Σp₁w/Σp₀w × 100. Suffix 0 = base year, 1 = current year.
**Laspeyre's** uses base-year quantities; **Paasche's** uses current-year quantities; **Fisher's** = geometric mean of the two – the **ideal index**.
**Time reversal test:** P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1 (ignore × 100). **Factor reversal test:** P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₀ (**true value ratio**). Fisher's index satisfies **both**.
Measures the effect of price changes on the cost of living of different classes – the change in income needed to keep the same standard of living. Also called consumer price index.
Uses: shows whether real wages rise or fall; used to regulate dearness allowance or bonus.
**Aggregate expenditure method** (price & quantity given): Σp₁q₀/Σp₀q₀ × 100 (same as Laspeyre's).
**Family budget method** (price & weight given): ΣPV/ΣV, P = p₁/p₀ × 100, V = p₀q₀ (weighted average of price relatives).
Quality depends on **4 M's** – Material, Manpower, Machines, Management. **Walter A. Shewhart** – father of SQC.

Causes of variation: **chance (random) causes** – small, natural, inherent, beyond human control (rain, floods, power cuts); **assignable causes** – non-random: defective raw material, faulty machines, unskilled manpower, worn-out tools, new operation. SQC aims to eliminate assignable causes.

**Process control** – minimising defectives during production using **control charts**. **Product control** – controlling quality of the finished product by **sampling inspection plans**; ensures the product sold does not contain many defectives.
**Control chart** (Shewhart): Centre Line (CL), Upper Control Limit (UCL), Lower Control Limit (LCL). All points within limits → process **in control**; any point outside → **out of control**.
Charts for variables: **mean (X̄) chart** – shows quality averages of samples; **range (R) chart** – shows variability/dispersion of samples.

terms: Long-term general tendency of a series to increase, decrease or stagnate.
Periodic variation within a year due to seasons, customs, festivals.
Oscillation over periods of more than a year (business cycle).
Random, unpredictable variation like floods, strikes.
Seasonal average expressed as a percentage of the grand average.
Statistical measure of relative change in a variable over time with a base period.
Index showing change in cost to maintain the same standard of living.
Natural, uncontrollable small causes of variation.
Identifiable non-random causes like faulty machines or bad material.
Chart with CL, UCL and LCL to check whether a process is in control.

q2.a: "A Time Series consists of data arranged chronologically" – Croxton & Cowden. "When quantitative data are arranged in the order of their occurrence, the resulting series is called the Time Series" – Wessel & Wallet.

q2.q: What is the need for studying time series?
q2.a: It helps in the analysis of past behaviour, in forecasting and future plans, in evaluating current achievements, and in comparative studies between one time period and others.

q2.q: Mention the components of the time series.
q2.a: (i) Secular trend (ii) Seasonal variations (iii) Cyclic variations (iv) Irregular variations.

Secular trend is a general tendency of a time series to increase or decrease or stagnate during a long period of time, e.g. upward tendency in population, production, sales; downward tendency in deaths, epidemics, mortality rate.
Seasonal index is the seasonal (monthly or quarterly) average expressed as a percentage of the grand average: S.I. = Seasonal average ÷ Grand average × 100.

q2.q: State the two normal equations used in fitting a straight line.
q2.a: ΣY = na + bΣX and ΣXY = aΣX + bΣX², where n is the number of years. When ΣX = 0, a = ΣY/n and b = ΣXY/ΣX².

q2.q: State the different methods of measuring trend.
q2.a: (i) Freehand or graphic method (ii) Method of semi-averages (iii) Method of moving averages (iv) Method of least squares.
"An Index Number is a device which shows by its variations the changes in a magnitude which is not capable of accurate measurements in itself or of direct valuation in practice" – Wheldon.

q2.q: State the uses of Index Number.
q2.a: (i) It is an important tool for formulating decisions and management policies. (ii) It helps in studying trends and tendencies. (iii) It determines inflation and deflation in an economy.

q2.q: Mention the classification of Index Number.
q2.a: (i) Price index number (ii) Quantity index number (iii) Cost of living index number.
Laspeyre's price index uses base-year quantities as weights: P₀₁ᴸ = Σp₁q₀/Σp₀q₀ × 100.
Paasche's price index uses current-year quantities as weights: P₀₁ᴾ = Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₁ × 100.

q2.q: State the test of adequacy of index number.
q2.a: (i) Time reversal test (ii) Factor reversal test. A good index number should satisfy both; Fisher's index satisfies both and is called the ideal index.
It tests the time consistency of an index number by working both forward and backward with respect to time: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1 (ignoring the factor 100).
The ratio between the total value of the current period and the total value of the base period, Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₀, is known as the true value ratio.
In this method the weights are values V = Σp₀q₀ of the base year, and cost of living index = ΣPV/ΣV, where P = (p₁/p₀) × 100 is the price relative. It is used when prices and weights are given.

q2.q: State the uses of Cost of Living Index Number.
q2.a: (i) It indicates whether the real wages of workers are rising or falling. (ii) It is used by administrators for regulating dearness allowance or grant of bonus to workers.

Statistical quality control is the application of statistical techniques to ensure quality specifications all along from the arrival of raw materials through processing to final delivery; quality depends on the 4 M's – Material, Manpower, Machines and Management.

q2.q: Mention the types of causes for variation in a production process.
q2.a: (1) Chance causes (random causes) (2) Assignable causes.
Small variations which are natural and inherent in the manufacturing process, beyond human control and which cannot be prevented, are chance (random) causes, e.g. rain, floods, power cuts.
Variation due to non-random causes which can occur at any stage of production, e.g. defective raw materials, fault in machines, unskilled manpower, worn-out tools, new operation.

q2.q: What do you mean by product control?
q2.a: Product control means controlling the quality of the product by critical examination through sampling inspection plans; it ensures the product sold does not contain a large number of defectives.

q2.q: What do you mean by process control?
q2.a: Process control is controlling and maintaining a satisfactory quality level during production by minimising the proportion of defectives, achieved through control charts.
A control chart (Shewhart) is a simple technique for detecting patterns of variation in data. It consists of a centre line (CL), an upper control limit (UCL) and a lower control limit (LCL).

q2.q: Name the control charts for variables.
q2.a: (i) Chart for mean (X̄ chart) (ii) Chart for range (R chart).
The X̄ chart is used to show the quality averages of the samples taken from the given process.
The R chart is used to show the variability or dispersion of the samples taken from the given process; R = x_max – x_min.

q2.q: Write the control limits for the mean chart.
q2.a: When σ is given: UCL = X̿ + 3σ/√n, CL = X̿, LCL = X̿ – 3σ/√n. When not given: UCL = X̿ + A₂R̄, CL = X̿, LCL = X̿ – A₂R̄.

q2.q: Write the control limits for the R chart.
q2.a: UCL = D₄R̄, CL = R̄, LCL = D₃R̄ (when σ is not given); when σ is given UCL = R̄ + 3σ_R, LCL = R̄ – 3σ_R.

q3.q: Write a brief note on seasonal variations
q3.a:
- Seasonal variations are movements due to nature which **repeat periodically in every season**, within a period of **less than one year**.
- They are influenced by natural forces, social customs and traditions and rise and fall uniformly and regularly.
- Examples: sale of umbrellas and raincoats in rainy season, cool drinks in summer, crackers in Deepawali, dresses in festival season, sugarcane in Pongal season.

q3.q: Explain cyclic variations
q3.a:
- Cyclic variations are not necessarily uniformly periodic; they may or may not follow exactly similar patterns after equal intervals.
- Generally one cyclic period ranges from **7 to 9 years**; there is no hard and fast rule.
- Example: the business cycle – start, boom, depression, recovery; changes in monetary policy and interest rates.

q3.q: Discuss about irregular variation
q3.a:
- Irregular variations have **no particular pattern** and no regular period of occurrence.
- They are accidental changes, purely random or unpredictable, normally short-term, but sometimes so intense that they give rise to new cyclic movements.
- Examples: floods, wars, earthquakes, tsunami, strikes, lockouts.

q3.q: Explain the method of fitting a straight line.
q3.a:
- By the **method of least squares**, the line of best fit Y = a + bX satisfies Σ(Y – Ŷ) = 0 and Σ(Y – Ŷ)² is least.
- The constants are found from the normal equations ΣY = na + bΣX and ΣXY = aΣX + bΣX².
- Taking the middle year as origin, ΣX = 0, so a = ΣY/n (mean of Y) and b = ΣXY/ΣX² (rate of change). For even years, X = (x – A.M. of middle years)/0.5.
- Substituting a and b gives the trend line and trend values.

q3.q: Write note on Fisher's price index number.
q3.a:
- Fisher's price index is the geometric mean of Laspeyre's and Paasche's indices: P₀₁ᶠ = √(P₀₁ᴸ × P₀₁ᴾ) = √[(Σp₁q₀ × Σp₁q₁)/(Σp₀q₀ × Σp₀q₁)] × 100.
- It uses both base-year and current-year quantities.
- It satisfies both the time reversal test and the factor reversal test, so it is termed an **ideal index number**.

q3.q: Explain Factor Reversal Test.
q3.a:
- The product of the price index number and the quantity index number from the base year to the current year should equal the **true value ratio**: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₀.
- Q₀₁ is obtained by interchanging p and q in the price index formula.
- Fisher's index satisfies this test.

q3.q: Discuss about Cost of Living Index Number.
q3.a:
- It is constructed to study the effect of changes in the price of goods and services on consumers for a current period compared with the base period.
- It measures the change in income necessary to maintain the same standard of living; since consumption habits differ between classes and regions, it is prepared for particular classes of people.
- Methods: **aggregate expenditure method** Σp₁q₀/Σp₀q₀ × 100 and **family budget method** ΣPV/ΣV.
- Uses: shows rise/fall of real wages; used to regulate dearness allowance and bonus.

q3.q: What are the uses of statistical quality control?
q3.a:
- Helps to diagnose lack of quality in raw materials, processes and machines.
- Helps to detect and eliminate assignable causes and keep the process under control (process control).
- Ensures that products sold to customers meet expected quality and do not contain many defectives (product control).
- Used in industries like automobiles, textiles, electrical equipment, biscuits, soaps, chemicals and petroleum.
